Chay Bowes: The Russian propaganda and disinformation that landed Irish man on an EU blacklist

Once known for exposing Leo Varadkar’s GP contract leak, Bowes is now under EU sanctions.

9.01am, 21 Nov 2026

Share options

Stephen McDermott

IN AUGUST 2024, a short clip circulated online claiming that Reporters Without Borders (RWB) had discovered widespread sympathy for Nazism among Ukrainian soldiers fighting against Russia.

It featured the BBC’s iconic logo in its top-left corner and relayed the story through white captions over grainy images of troops from the front and blurred helmets with SS badges.

As the video cut briskly through grainy frontline stills, its authoritative BBC watermark and crisp white captions seamlessly mimicked a legitimate news dispatch, claiming RWB had uncovered 1,000 cases where combatants had donned Nazi symbols and that the group had called on other media organisations to cover the story. 

But this was not a legitimate BBC report, and RWB never made such a finding.

In a subsequent investigation, the press-freedom group found that the clip was an example of literal fake news promoted by pro-Russian accounts on X and Telegram.

Their report said the video was initially posted by an anonymous account on X called ‘Patricia’, but that one of the first people to pick it up and amplify it was Irishman Chay Bowes.

From there, it went viral across a network of Russian propagandists and the country’s foreign embassies, and was mentioned at a press conference by Maria Zakharova, the official spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry.

Bowes – who first entered the public eye as the whistleblower in the 2020 Leo Varadkar GP contract leak before co-founding The Ditch website – now works for Russian state broadcaster RT and was among 30 individuals sanctioned by the European Union this week.

Announcing the sanctions, the Council of the EU described Bowes and three other media figures as “propagandists”, saying they had participated in information manipulation and spread narratives “that legitimise and sustain” Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Under the measures, Bowes’s EU-based assets are frozen and EU citizens and companies are banned from providing him with funds. He is also prohibited from entering or transiting through EU member states, though this doesn’t include Ireland.

In justifying the sanctions, the council pointed to his work hosting the RT programme “Moscow Mules”,alongside his co-founding of the pro-Russian disinformation network The Islander News.

It also cited his participation in influence operations run by the Wagner Group-founded Foundation to Battle Injustice, as well as his “spreading of anti-Western and anti-Ukraine disinformation” during a 2023 appearance at the UN Security Council on Russia’s behalf.

It said that through these activites, he was “facilitating actions or policies attributable” to the government of Russia which “undermine or threaten democracy, the rule of law, stability or security” in the European Union.

Bowes criticised the move on social media as anti-free speech and an attempt to “bully me into silence”, while People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd-Barrett also labelled it “a sinister development”.

In a brief response to queries from The Journal this week, he said that he considers the sanctions to be “illegal and utterly baseless” and described allegations that he had spread disinformation on behalf of Russian groups as “false”.

Bowes and his defenders have framed the sanctions as an attack on press freedom.

Critics such as People Before Profit have warned that penalising commentators without a trial creates a dangerous slippery slope for free expression, likening it to US sanctions against UN Special Rapporteur for Palestine Francesca Albanese.

The EU though believes its decision is justified following a years-long trail of fabricated stories and Kremlin-aligned disinformation about the war in Ukraine.

Bowes’ journey raises questions about how a figure who first made his name scrutinising Irish politics became such a prolific amplifier of Russian government talking points in the West.

A still from the fake BBC News clipX.com

‘A long line of Irish people queued up to shake his hand’

To understand how a Dublin-born businessman ended up on an EU sanctions list alongside Russian state operatives, it helps to trace a career built on continuous reinvention – one that began not in Russia, but in the Irish medical sector.

Long before Bowes began broadcasting from Moscow, he came into the Irish public’s consciousness as a healthcare entrepreneur turned whistleblower.

In 2017, he co-founded Community Hospital Ireland, a private company that provided healthcare in patients’ homes and reinvested profits into treatment for chronic illness.

The venture brought him into contact with Galway doctor Maitiú Ó Tuathail, then president of the National Association of General Practitioners (NAGP), a now-defunct union for GPs.

The relationship brought NAGP support to CHI, and by 2019, the two were close enough that Ó Tuathail felt comortable sending Bowes a message that showed he had obtained a confidential GP contract between the government and the Irish Medical Organisation.

The young doctor had received a copy of the contract from an acquaintance, then-Taoiseach Leo Varadkar, boasting to Bowes about how he acquired it in a text message: “To be fair, Leo always delivers.”

Leo Varadkar become embroiled in controversy after Chay Bowes revealed he had leaked a GP contractAlamy

Through Web Summit founder Paddy Cosgrave, Bowes teamed up with Village magazine, which published what became known as the ‘Leo the leak’ exposé in 2020 – much of it relying on Bowes’ text messages and documents.

“I was dumbfounded that a friend of the then-Taoiseach was claiming such professional closeness to him that he would improperly forward him potentially explosive confidential documentation,” he told the magazine at the time.

The ensuing political controversy earned Bowes genuine goodwill among a cohort of Irish readers as someone who had helped reveal how the most senior figure in the government did a secret favour for someone in his personal inner circle.

The following year, Cosgrave invited Bowes and Village editor Michael Smith to the stage during the opening of the Web Summit in Lisbon and urged the audience to give them a round of applause.

“@BowesChay spoke on stage at @WebSummit about @LeoVaradkar after which a long line of Irish people queued up to shake his hand,” Cosgrave gushed on Twitter afterwards.

Paddy Cosgrave's tweet about Chay Bowes at the Web SummitX.com / @paddycosgrave

X.com / @paddycosgrave / @paddycosgrave

The episode exposed a combative streak that defined Bowes’s early public life: a readiness to sever personal alliances so that he could challenge institutional power, regardless of the fallout.

The same year as his Web Summit appearance, he parlayed the profile he had attained from his involvement in the ‘Leo the leak’ story by co-founding investigative website The Ditch, alongside journalists Eoghan McNeill and Roman Shortall.

The venture, which initially received financial backing from Cosgrave, cemented his reputation as a relentless, if opportunistic, scrutineer of Irish political power given how many stories they broke about Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil politicians. 

Bowes subsequently resigned as director of and sold his shares in The Ditch in June 2022, before the outlet’s reporting led to the resignations of An Bórd Pleanála deputy chairman Paul Hyde and government junior ministers Damien English and Robert Troy, the latter of whom has since returned to government. 

‘It is simplistic to cast Russia as a deviant nation’

The audience that Bowes built through his role in Ireland’s alternative and independent media between 2020 and 2022 showed his relentless appetite for challenging domestic political orthodoxy.

Soon he began to apply that same contrarian, anti-establishment lens to Western foreign policy.

As the pandemic subsided and Russia prepared to invade Ukraine, the one-time whistleblower’s attention began to shift noticeably to more geopolitical interests.

CNN's homepage on the day Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022Alamy

It was not entirely new ground for Bowes; three years earlier, he had published an essay in the Dublin-based independent magazine Cassandra Voices, taking aim at Nato expansion and criticising EU leaders seeking to absorb Ukraine into the “Western orbit”.

Returning to this theme in January 2022, a month before Russia’s full-scale invasion, he published another essay in which he argued that Ireland – due to its history of partition, ethnic division, and proximity to a powerful neighbour – is uniquely positioned to understand the complexities of the Ukraine-Russia conflict.

He presented the looming conflict through the prism of a crisis rooted in the expansion of Nato and a failure to recognise Russia’s legitimate security interests.

“It is simplistic to cast Russia as a deviant nation hellbent on suppressing and oppressing its neighbours, particularly those previously a part of the Soviet Union,” he wrote.

“The truth is far more complex.”

Yet in February 2022, Bowes’s initial reaction was notably equivocal on what was unfolding at Europe’s eastern border.

When Russia invaded Ukraine in the early hours of 24 February 2022, he took to Twitter to say he didn’t accept the country’s actions or find them acceptable.

His criticism was couched in qualified support for Ukraine (“I am 100% against any action [...] that causes loss of life”) and posts that took as much aim at Nato and the United States as they did at Russia.

Bowes Twitter thread from the morning of 24 February 2022X.com / @BowesChay

X.com / @BowesChay / @BowesChay

There were also times when his criticism of Russia was more categorical.

At one point early in the war, he described what was happening as “immoral” and said that Russia had carried out an “illegal and brutal invasion” that was leading to the “murder” of Ukrainian citizens.

“This entirely unacceptable and unnecessary war in #Ukraine is entirely unjustified and unjustifiable,” he posted.

It was a viewpoint that wasn’t to last.

Over the following year, Bowes’ Twitter feed shifted incrementally from condemning Russia to questioning Western support, moving first through amplification and selective framing rather than fabrication.

In May 2022, he shared a Bloomberg opinion column asking whether then-UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson was prolonging the war; in January 2023, he cited a genuine US State Department human-rights report in a post that argued against funding and arming Kyiv.

Even on 31 August 2022, he still affirmed Ukraine’s right to freedom and statehood, though he did so alongside criticism of Volodymyr Zelenskyy and claims that Kyiv was persecuting Russian speakers in the Donbass region.

Ten months on, appearing via video link at a June 2023 UN Security Council briefing, he had shed all nuance in favour of an unabashedly pro-Kremlin line. 

Invited by Russia, Bowes – given the on-screen title of “scholar specialising in small arms and munitions” - addressed the UN’s highest-authority body and cast Russian troops as “defenders” and Ukraine as a “chaotic and essentially failed state”.

He used his appearance to shift blame for the ongoing bloodshed squarely onto Western capitals.

“Settlement will come, and it is my absolute belief that it is up to those in Washington DC and London, now fuelling the conflict with endless escalatory military aid to Ukraine, to decide where and when that settlement occurs, either at the negotiating table or on the battlefield,” he said.

While Russian ambassador Vassily Nebenzia publicly thanked him afterwards, the next speaker – Soviet-born British historian Sergey Radchenko – rebuked him by name.

Bowes, he said, had come to the UN chamber to lecture delegates on “how terrible it is to support a victim of unprovoked aggression, how terrible it is to help people under attack, how terrible it is to resist imperialist conquest”.

Chay Bowes appears on screen at the UN Security Council in June 2023United Nations

United Nations

Moscow Mules

By tracing Bowes’s odyssey from nuanced early reaction to the war in early 2022 to unambiguous pro-Kremlin, West-critical posturing at the UN 18 months later, one can see how his public pronouncements coincided with his changing professional orbit.

After giving up his work and shares in The Ditch in June 2022, the former whistleblower moved to Moscow in the latter half of that year to become a correspondent for RT.

Even at that stage, the state-funded outlet (previously known as Russia Today) had become an outcast in the broadcasting world on foot of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Brussels sanctioned RT as a state propaganda outlet, and it was banned across the European Union, stripped of its broadcasting licence in the United Kingdom, and blocked from platforms including YouTube, Meta, Google, Apple and TikTok.

But the company gave Bowes an institutional standing and media salary, while also enabling him to continue his anti-establishment talking points against European politicians, the US and Nato.

He was not the first Western figure to take up a role with the broadcaster.

Since the early 2010s, RT has opportunistically recruited Western anti-establishment figures with offers of generous pay and editorial freedom “as a way of authenticating the messaging they want to promote”, according to Stephen Hutchings, professor of Russian studies at the University of Manchester.

Those hired were not necessarily dupes, he explains, but commentators who “saw RT as an opportunity for them to promote their agendas”.

Hutchings notes that the 2022 bans pushed RT into far more overt propaganda, blending contradictions that cast Russia simultaneously as an anti-imperialist champion, a victim of Western cultural colonisation and a great power entitled to its own sphere of influence.

“These three lines don’t really hang together, but that doesn’t matter,” he says.

“You pick whichever of those messages works best for a particular audience or in a particular situation.”

Bowes began his career with RT as a correspondent, appearing in news segments to provide his analysis of global events, in clips that were also shared on social media.

ICYMI: Pentagon Investigates Major Leak Of 'Classified Documents'

Washington is alarmed after a new trove of secret US national security documents relating to Ukraine, China & the Middle East appeared online. 

RT correspondent Chay Bowes is in the studio to explain the events. https://t.co/AQoLHw5WRi— RT_India (@RT_India_news) April 9, 2023

By early 2024, he had been given his own sleekly-edited weekly podcast, Moscow Mules, with targets including EU countries and their leadership, US politics, the Russia-Ukraine war, and domestic affairs in Ireland and the United Kingdom.

Alongside sleek editing, the show adopts a faux-casual, smirking register – using derisive humour as a delivery mechanism to launder hard-edged Kremlin talking points.

A recent episode called ‘The unflushed empire’ examined claims that a foreign power could be behind recent home intrusions targeting 20 members of Finland’s parliament; amid suggestions that the intruders had left behind unflushed toilets and human waste, the episode ironically dismissed the claim by calling it Operation Number Two.

The framing sought to dismiss the story as yet another attempt by the West to blame the Kremlin on even trivial things, a play that helps to undermine criticism of more globally consequential activities by Russia. 

Between these instances of so-called satire, however, have been plenty of cases where Bowes has leaned into Russian disinformation narratives.

In a November 2025 broadcast titled ‘A fool and his money’, the programme suggested that Western financial support for Kyiv is a giant fraud, promising to show how “EU elites and Ukroscammers enjoy revelling in free taxpayer money”.

Framing Western military and financial assistance to Ukraine as an embezzlement scheme is one of the Kremlin’s main anti-Ukraine narratives, designed to turn EU and US citizens against supporting Kyiv and to derail the country’s EU accession.

In another episode from August, Bowes appeared on-screen beside an article from a website called the Irish Sun, reporting corruption allegations involving Zelenskyy’s staff.

Despite its name, the site is an online outlet operated by an Australian company, Midwest Radio Network, on behalf of its Dubai-based parent company, Big News Network.

It was set up in 2002 and claims to take its name from a newspaper that was published in Ireland from 1880, and explicitly disclaims any connection to the Murdoch-owned newspaper of the same name.

“Irish Sun is not associated with The Sun in the UK, or that publication’s Irish edition,” its ‘about page’ says.

Big News Network, which supplies the site’s syndicated content, is an international syndication network identified by disinformation researchers as a “pink slime” operation that republishes sanctioned Russian state media. 

The Irish Sun article used by Bowes visibly credited RT.com, allowing the segment to function like a digital hall of mirrors.

Kremlin-aligned copy left Moscow via RT, passed through an Australian-owned aggregator donning an Irish masthead, and bounced straight back onto Bowes’s studio screen in Russia as apparent third-party corroboration.

Advertisement

Source: RT.com

The show has also repeatedly pushed the pretext for Russia’s invasion by claiming that Ukrainian state bodies are partnering with neo-Nazis and that Volodymyr Zelenskyy is an “unelected dictator” presiding over a corrupt regime.

Ukrainian volunteer militias with far-right roots like the Azov Battalion were once active in the country, but were formally absorbed into the country’s regular military structure over a decade ago.

While far-right elements persist within pockets of the armed forces, researchers note they remain a small minority rather than a state-controlling force, with one calling them a “proverbial drop in the ocean”.

Zelenskyy remains in office because Ukrainian law prohibits holding elections under martial law during a foreign invasion.

It’s an arrangement that has occasionally prompted debate inside Ukraine, but has been navigated through constitutional consensus, regular parliamentary votes, and the view that a ballot must wait until peacetime.

One episode description recently labelled Zelenskyy as the “Cocainefuhrer”, linking the claim that he is an unelected Nazi to an ongoing smear by Russia that the Ukrainian leader is a drug addict.

The misinformation spread on Moscow Mules is not just limited to the conflict in Ukraine.

In the same October 2026 episode mocking the Finnish break-ins, an episode description claimed that Met Police in London had been “traded for Sharia patrols”, reviving a long-debunked far-right trope that suggests that parts of the British capital have ceded control of their streets to Islamic religious police.

“What you definitely can’t do is drink a beer near a mosque because, of course, Islam is the national religion of the UK now,” he told viewers, introducing a clip taken from social media where a man asks a group not to consume alcohol on a street.

“Imagine a white British Christian went and complained about this type of stuff that’s also happening in the UK right now; think about what would happen [...] Six months in prison? Hate crime? Racism? Nazi? You get the picture.”

Another episode criticised USAID as US taxpayer money going “down the drain of the clogged bathrooms of transgender Colombian operas”.

It echoed a White House and DOGE talking point that cited a purported “$47,000 (€43,000) grant for a ‘transgender opera’ in Colombia” as proof of “waste and abuse” to justify dismantling USAID, though spending records show USAID gave no money to the project.

Elon Musk wearing a DOGE baseball cap in the White HouseAlamy

The Islander News

When EU bans at the outset of the war cut RT off from the European airwaves, Moscow’s messaging apparatus required a more ostensibly independent vehicle to reach Western readers.

Bowes helped to fill this gap through The Islander News, another website he founded in recent years.

His involvement in the project served as a key justification for his recent sanctioning by the EU council.

The legal text of the council’s decision specifically highlighted his work on the outlet, which bills itself as offering “deep geopolitical analysis” and “long-form op-eds” aimed at a “more just world order” on Telegram and Substack.

Like Moscow Mules, The Islander’s primary focus is anti-Western, Kremlin-aligned commentary.

It targets Ukraine and EU institutions, and has also sought to undermine elections in countries on Russia’s periphery.

During contested elections in Georgia and Moldova last year, Bowes framed pro-democracy protests in Tbilisi as an attempted “coup”, while The Islander also amplified unsubstantiated claims of voter suppression and warmongering against Moldova’s pro-EU government.

Bowes criticising Moldova in similar terms to his criticism of UkraineX.com

The outlet has also come under fire for its stance on the invasion of Ukraine, particularly through its laundering and amplification of narratives pushed by Storm-1516, a Russian-affiliated disinformation and influence operation.

In May last year, a report by Vignium – France’s state agency tasked with detecting foreign digital interference – found that the “vast majority” of Storm-1516 narratives were amplified by social media accounts and websites belonging to four named individuals.

One of those individuals was Bowes, with the report including his handle on X and the URL of The Islander featuring alongside his name.

The report said that The Islander was “considered likely to have been paid for or activated by” malicious actors within the Russian information manipulation sector.

“Vignium notes that most of these actors have close links with Russian organisations with a long history of information operations targeting foreign audiences,” the report says.

One of the Storm-1516 narratives identified by Vignium was a false claim from November 2023 that Zelenskyy had bought two luxury yachts worth $75 million (€68 million).

Debunking the story, the Associated Press established that both yachts remained for sale and that the purported sales documents contained outdated branding, and specifically named the Islander as publishing the claim. 

Another report by Clemson University in South Carolina also found that Bowes had, through The Islander, shared multiple narratives from Storm-1516 and the Foundation to Battle Injustice, a second Russian disinformation and influence operation founded by the since-deceased Wagner Group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin.

Wagner Group founder Yevgeny PrigozhinAlamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Russian influence campaigns rely on ostensibly independent sites and trusted Western commentators to give fabricated stories “the appearance of legitimacy” and reach audiences predisposed to believe them, explains Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University’s Media Forensics Hub.

Disinformation experts call this process information laundering, a tactic in which state-backed propaganda is routed through seemingly independent third-party outlets to obscure its origins, before appearing to Western audiences as credible news.

Between 2023 and 2024, Linvill says, Bowes’s routine sharing of Storm-1516 claims across The Islander and social media made him, for a time, “Russia’s leading mouthpiece in sharing this set of lies”.

Bowes has said that he is no longer involved in The Islander.

It is reported that he gave control of the project to Nolan in the first half of 2024, a timeline consistent with the fact that The Islander’s newer X account (created in July 2024) lists Nolan as its sole owner.

Even with that shift in ownership, Brussels’ citing of both RT and The Islander in its 16 November decision to sanction Bowes highlights their distinct roles in his wider output.

Although RT operates as a heavily branded, state-stamped broadcast studio, which had been locked out of European airwaves, The Islander worked as a more shadowy operation.

By presenting itself as an independent Anglophone outlet, it managed to dress Kremlin up as impartial commentary to slip past sceptical Western readers on Telegram and Substack.

Ten narratives on X

Bowes continued to post similar claims on his personal channels, so articles and posts published under The Islander’s banner after the transfer of ownership in 2024 cannot be attributed to him.

That didn’t stop him from amplifying Storm-1516 elsewhere, particularly through his account on X.

An analysis by The Journal of his posts on the social media platform found that he promoted at least 10 other narratives identified by Vignium as originating from the group.

Several echoed the same formula as the yacht rumour, alleging extravagant purchases by Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife.

In October 2023, Bowes shared a now-deleted post – preserved in an online forum archive – referencing fabricated claims that Olena Zelenska had spent over $1 million (€910,000) at Cartier.

Over the following year and a half, he also helped circulate bogus stories that the Zelenskyys had bought a luxury Bugatti, Sting’s Tuscan estate, France’s Milleis bank, and – according to researchers tracking German election interference – Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a frequent target of BowesAlamy

Bowes did not always present such claims as established fact.

He openly noted that documents in a post regarding Milleis bank – subsequently debunked by AFP – were uncertain or “unverified”.

“A French video is circulating alleging Zelenskys offshore company was involved in buying a French Bank,” he said on X.

“The unverified report says Milleis Banque was bought via his offshore Co. Maltex for approx €1.2B.”

Other posts targeted high-profile figures and major international events.

In early 2024, he promoted a fabricated story of a Ukrainian plot to assassinate Tucker Carlson, before sharing a smear falsely claiming Russian opposition figure Leonid Volkov was attacked by a former lover.

That July, a post amplifying a fake Hamas threat against the Paris Olympics racked up nearly three million views.

Storm-1516’s Western election narratives also featured prominently on Bowes’ X feed.

Ahead of the US presidential election in October 2024, he shared a fabricated claim accusing Kamala Harris of cocaine addiction.

Months later, during Germany’s federal election, he circulated a staged video falsely purporting to show postal ballots for the far-right AfD being shredded.

That pattern continued between May and July 2025 during an influence push targeting Moldova.

In surviving posts later mapped by researchers, Bowes promote an allegation traced back to the Foundation to Battle Injustice via the fringe outlet Veterans Today.

His focus on European ballots also drew direct pushback inside the EU in May 2025, when Romanian authorities detained Bowes and denied him entry after he flew in from Dublin ahead of a controversial re-run of the country’s presidential election.

He was declared a “threat to the security of the state”, and subsequently boarded a flight to Istanbul.

Nor do his posts simply concern direct Russian interests.

In another study, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue identified Bowes as a frequent commentator on immigration in Ireland in ways that echo claims by Russian state media.

His posts included descriptions of immigration as a “scam” and critiques of the Irish government for giving housing and financial support to Ukrainian refugees, alongside claims that the Ukrainian government was a “corrupted dictatorship”.

“While of course entitled to his personal opinions, it is interesting given his employment as an RT commentator that he selectively framed the Ukrainian government in terms aligning with Kremlin narratives,” the report said.

“With over 270,000 followers on X, his content is available to Irish audiences but is also frequently shared by other actors in pro-Kremlin online spaces.”

An anti-immigration protest in Dublin in 2024Alamy

Ciaran O’Connor, a senior analyst at the ISD, points out that Bowes – who recently labelled the EU “an authoritarian network of client states where sovereignty is a memory” – frequently frames migration as an EU-enforced “scam” imposed on Ireland from outside.

According to O’Connor, Bowes also taps into deeply felt domestic grievances in Ireland over housing, immigration and the cost of living in a manner that acts as a “gateway”.

He says this can build trust with local audiences who view Bowes as an independent voice, before gradually introducing them to Kremlin-aligned commentary on Russia and Ukraine they might never have sought out on their own.

Bowes has denied being associated with an influence operation or being paid to post material sympathetic to Russian views.

Clemson University’s Darren Linvill says there is a distinction between active state direction and willing amplification, noting he has seen no evidence that Bowes orchestrated Russian influence campaigns himself.

“I think the evidence points to him being a useful mouthpiece, not a mastermind,” he says.

Bowes has removed posts that contain misinformation, as he did with the fake BBC clip about Ukrainian Nazis once he was contacted by RSF.

‘No evidence, no hearing’

Eventually, Brussels decided that Bowes had crossed the line from contrarian commentator to active conduit for foreign interference.

The extensive trail of digital amplification landed him on the European Council’s sanctions list this week.

In its announcement, the council said the decision to target Bowes came amid the backdrop of “increasing Russian hybrid activities aimed at destabilising EU societies”. 

The move triggered severe practical consequences for Bowes, leading to his assets being frozen across the EU and a strict ban on EU citizens or entities providing him with funds.

The measures do not prevent him from returning to Ireland, but they effectively quarantine his financial and professional footprint within the EU.

Bowes has aggressively framed the move as an attack on fundamental rights, casting the sanctions as an authoritarian attempt to silence dissenting voices.

“The EU sanctioned me for being a ‘disinformation hub’,” he wrote on X afterwards.

“No evidence, no hearing, nothing. Now I can’t move around the EU, can’t bank, and can’t receive money. All because I challenged the Western narrative on Ukraine.”

Others rowed in to defend him, including former Independents4Change MEP Clare Daly, who described the sanctions as “extrajudicial punishment for disfavoured speech”, and the aforementioned TD Richard Boyd-Barrett, who claimed they were issued to a “journalist for not toeing [the] western line”.

People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd-BarrettAlamy

Their defence taps into a vital democratic question about an individual’s right to challenge prevailing orthodoxy.

But the documented trail of interference at such a heightened time would also lead to questions if Brussels didn’t act.

The council’s legal text surgically cited Bowes’ active involvement in “information manipulation” and his role as a key amplifier for operations like Storm-1516.

The threshold for sanctions was deemed to have been crossed not when Bowes voiced pro-Kremlin views, but when his commentary became, in the opinion of the European Council, a documented conduit for malicious foreign interference.

Bowes has framed the move as censorship, arguing on X that he was sanctioned without a hearing or evidence merely for offering “dissenting opinions”.

Gavin Barrett, professor of EU constitutional and economic law at University College Dublin’s Sutherland School of Law, notes that while EU measures must be legally reasoned, Bowes can challenge his listing before the EU courts in Luxembourg under Article 263 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

Any such challenge would likely invoke Article 11 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, which protects freedom of expression and media pluralism.

Yet Barrett notes that judges would weigh that protection against “times of massive media manipulation”, scrutinising his role at banned state broadcaster RT alongside posts sharing a fake BBC clip and a staged German ballot-shredding video.

“A court might well take the view that this kind of activity is far removed from the kind of legitimate journalistic activity intended to be protected by the Charter,” he says.

news.title: How Trump lost Joe Rogan in the manosphere meltdown
news.text:
“It was the pod bros wot won it.” That could easily have been the headline in 2024, after Donald Trump stormed to victory in the presidential election with the testosterone-drenched help of the podcast manosphere and, in particular, its loudest voice, Joe Rogan. 

Back then the podcast king, who the Wall Street Journal described as “the most influential swing voter in America”, endorsed Trump. Rogan’s influence has only increased since. In March 2024, his podcast The Joe Rogan Experience had 14.5 million followers on Spotify. That has since grown to around 18 million followers.

Alongside the likes of Tucker Carlson, former US Navy Seal Shawn Ryan and Dan Bongino, who served for nine months as Trump’s FBI deputy director, Rogan has become a leading light in the manosphere – a motley crew of podcasters and online influencers who became self-styled champions of traditional masculinity, anti-wokeism and, at one point, Maga politics. 

However, ahead of this month’s midterms, the 59-year-old comedian and wrestling commentator turned his back on the President. 

Trump “didn’t just lose the podcast bros”, said Rogan last week on his podcast, “he lost most of the country”. This assessment shows how the midterms not only upended the political geography of America, but also marked a shift in a conservative media ecosystem that used to be solid Maga.

No demographic turned out to be more pivotal in the presidential election two years ago than men aged between 18 and 29, 55 per cent of whom backed Trump over his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris. Support for Trump among young white men, millions of whom listen to Rogan and his fellow Maga-friendly podcasters, was even higher, at 63 per cent. 

In the midterm elections, however, at least 59 per cent of men aged from 18 to 29 voted Democrat, a massive swing away from the Republicans. Not only should we be talking of a blue tsunami but also a right-wing manosphere meltdown. 

Rogan, in his election post-mortem, itemised why one-time Maga supporters had deserted the President’s party. Number one was “a war that no one wants to be in”.

Rogan also hit back against the Trump’s administration’s crackdown on unauthorised immigrants by “militarised police in the streets wearing masks”. It was not, he said, “a good thing to snatch people up out of their f**king taco stand that have been in the country for 20 years”.

He has previously criticised the administration’s handling of the Epstein files and the Trump family’s money-making crypto schemes. 

All this was a far cry from 2024, when a week-and-a-half from Election Day Trump spent almost three hours chatting on air to Rogan about everything from UFOs to wind farms, the possibility of life on Mars to the military tactics of Confederate General Robert E Lee, which he likened to UFC cage fighters.

That episode garnered 25 million listens, and more than 50 million downloads on YouTube, and came to be regarded as one of the most important media events of the 2024 election campaign – up there with Joe Biden’s catastrophic televised debate performance and the assassination attempt on Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania. 

Two years ago, the manosphere media blitz became a central prong of Trump’s campaign strategy to regain the presidency. Trump not only appeared with Rogan but took part in more than a dozen podcasts, including Theo Von’s This Past Weekend, Andrew Schulz’s Flagrant, the Full Send Podcast from the Nelk Boys, Bussin’ With The Boys, a sports podcast hosted by former NFL players Will Compton and Taylor Lewan, Logan Paul’s Impaulsive show and Adin Ross’s Stream.

But in this election cycle, Trump did not appear on a single one of their shows. 

Even before the Republican rout, Trump aides from the 2024 campaign were sounding the alarm. “If we don’t win it will be because the President’s staff failed to execute his winning playbook in 2024,” warned former Trump communications specialist Caroline Sunshine in late October. “We’re not on podcasts, we’re not talking to that audience… Hey guys, we need to go talk to Joe Rogan.” 

Trump’s lack of appearance may be because he had come to regard himself as the “influencer-in-chief”. The White House also knew many of the manosphere presenters had become hostile. Theo Von, who presents the number 2 show on Spotify, with five million monthly listeners, has labelled the Iran war “diabolical,” “insane,” “sick,” “f**king baffling”, and “dark”.

Another critic is Adin Ross, the internet celebrity who in 2024 famously presented Trump with a Rolex watch and customised Tesla Cybertruck emblazoned with the iconic shot of Trump punching the air after surviving the assassination attempt in Pennsylvania. Ross evidently suffered “eight figure” losses on the stock market following Trump’s Liberation Day tariff spree and announced on a livestream last September that he regretted ever venturing into politics and associating himself with Trump. 

Like Ross, Schulz, another manosphere influencer, also broke with the President prior to the start of the Iran war. In July 2025, Schulz complained Trump was “doing the exact opposite of everything I voted for”. He added: “I want him to stop the wars. He’s funding them. I want him to shrink spending, reduce the budget. He’s increasing it.”

The moustachioed comedian has also been critical of Trump’s handling of the Epstein files. Since the midterms, on his Brilliant Idiots podcast, Schulz has accused the Trump administration of “corruption and cronyism that has never been seen in Western democracy” and hit out at Trump as “the greatest failure of a President of our lifetime”.

The Trump administration has previously said: “Neither the President nor his family has ever engaged – or will ever engage – in conflicts of interest.” It recently added that Trump acts only with the best interests of the American people in mind.

Other than illustrating the deep anger towards the President, and the sense of betrayal over Iran, what does this tell us about US political culture? Certainly it speaks of the split evident at this election, in which voters loosened their affiliation to the Republican Party and the Maga movement without necessarily developing a firm attachment to the Democrats. It also demonstrates what’s called horseshoe politics, where the right and left are often not that far apart, like the tips of a horseshoe. 

Manosphere podcasters are not as ideological, and therefore not as set on to the Republican Party as conservative shock jocks of the past, such as Rush Limbaugh, whom Trump awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2020. Limbaugh, for instance, remained a staunch supporter of George W Bush’s deeply unpopular Iraq war.

Then there is the profit motive: the dollars and cents, which may have turned influencers into followers. Brian Rosenwald, the author of Talk Radio America: How an Industry took over a Political Party that took over the United States, told CNN that “few hosts of any stripe are going to do something that puts them on the wrong side of their audience – which threatens the bottom line”.

That is a financial rationale that Trump himself would understand. 

But over the course of this century, American voters have become far more fickle. Three one-term presidencies have followed three two-term presidencies. In 12 out of the 14 elections, the White House, the House or the Senate have changed hands. The podcast manosphere speaks of this political whiplash. The Joe Rogan Experience is being mirrored across the land.

news.title: Tony Deyal | Trump and follow shoot
news.text:
When I was a youngster with my neighbours heading for school, we loved, “Cricket lovely cricket.” And some of us still do. But basically, the cricket came second when President Donald Trump famously declared on the campaign trail, “I know words … I have the best words.”

The “Trump” phrase became a central point of media attention, political satire, and analysis of his distinct rhetorical style. For that man and others who loved Trump as a fantastic political “BOSS”, there was “Playing a Trump” (“Ruffing”). If you do not have any cards in the ‘led suit’, you could choose to play a “Trump” card to win the trick, especially against the others (known as “ruffing”). You can also take a card from a different plain suit even if that was hidden or ‘grabbed’ from someone else. Even if there were no Trump played, the biggest card of the original led suit wins.

Word was, with “Trump”, he supposedly always wins regardless. As “Donald John Trump”, he was an American politician, media personality, and businessman who became the 45th (2017-2021) and 47th (2025-present) president of the United States, first ran for president in 2000 as candidate for the Reform Party of the United States. He withdrew from the race before the primaries. Trump won the 2016 election running as the Republican Party nominee, despite losing the popular vote. Trump ran for re-election in 2020 but lost to former vice-president Joe Biden. He subsequently won the 2024 election against Vice-President Kamala Harris to serve a non-consecutive second term as president, again as a Republican candidate.

However, Donald Trump was seen as an unpopular president and lost many seats, including those affected by the soaring cost of living, the unpopular Iran war, Democrats, and Trump’s unpopularity was seen as a drag on Republicans. Then in his second time there were strong loyalists, early executive actions focused on immigration, federal regulations, and the economy, and ongoing policy initiatives. By that time, Trump was even seen as “Dumbest!”

For example, Trump told his people, “It’s called the bowling ball test. They take a bowling ball from 20 feet up in the air and drop it on the hood of the car ... If the hood dents, the car doesn’t qualify. It’s horrible.”

Then he said, “Airplanes are becoming far too complex to fly. Pilots are no longer needed, but rather computer scientists from MIT ... I don’t know about you, but I don’t want Albert Einstein to be my pilot.”

And if that was bad enough, he told them, “If you go out and you want to buy groceries, you need a picture on a card, you need ID ... You go out and you want to buy anything, you need ID and you need your picture.”

To end it, he came out with his best of all time: “I think one of the greatest of all terms I’ve come up with, ‘fake’ ... I guess other people have used it, perhaps, over the years, but I’ve never noticed it.”

From then it was clear that we can hear from Trump with, “Weekend Update Trump Admin Comments on FAA Outage ...” and “Long-time Trump employee speaks out about Trump’s documents including obstruction mails at Mar-a-Lago.”

Then almost immediately, “Trump is Hiding” and one person said, “Oh My God ...”

Then there were “TROUBLE FOR TRUMP”, “TRUMP IS DONE”, and “IMPEACH THIS CRIMINAL!” (most times it is Trump).

Then there were “NEW MAR-A-LAGO EVIDENCE” and that takes it to “SUPREME COURT DEFEATS HIM!”

But it always continued to go after Trump: “JUDGE ORDERS TRUMP TO TESTIFY!” (In his own lawsuit!).

Trump didn’t, but said, “IT’S ALL ABOUT THIS EGO!”

However, that seemed to be followed by “NEW EVIDENCE DISCLOSED!”

Then there came a “BREAKING NEWS” from a judge who just “ordered Trump ...”

But, as usual, Trump said, “I don’t know.”

Then almost immediately another judge asked, “ARE DOCUMENTS BEING DESTROYED?”

Worse is the “EPSTEIN FILES”, where there is “Enough evidence on Donald Trump.”

It was a “Bombshell Midterms ...”

At the same time, “HOW SCARED REPUBLICANS ARE OF TALKING ABOUT THE EPSTEIN FILES.”

Worse, there was even more: “Trump Cashes Out & Shifts Blame As After Dems Crush Maga ...”, “Trump Hopes for Heaven” on “60 Minutes & Stephen Miller.”

Then increasingly all the people became very clear: “IT’S ALL OVER! TRUMP.”

They also added, “Smoking gun”, “OH MY GOD”, and “IT’S ALL COMING OUT!”

It is at this point some of our friends told us to stop all that terrible “Trump, Trump” and give us a few jokes to ease us up for a while and only then come back with the Trump or “BOSS”.

However, they wanted to understand the whole Trump and what he did against the rest of all of us. So, we told them, “Great. Sit down, relax, and lime with us for a short while.”

In a way, we decided to get a bigger sense of life and existence. For example, Austin Taylor (On Infinity) said, “Two things are infinite: the universe and human stupidity; and I’m not sure about the universe.”

Mae West, on living, told us, “You only live once, but if you do it right, once is enough.”

Unfortunately, that is not how Trump went with it at any time.

Then Douglas Adams (On Creation) told us, “In the beginning, the Universe was created. This has made a lot of people very angry and been widely regarded as a bad move.”

Perhaps this is true.

However, Lily Tomlin (On Identity), which truly takes us back to Trump and others, said, “I always wanted to be somebody, but now I realise once is enough.”

We were going to add some more but we were told to go with something better, like funny and happy quotes about being important.

There were some great ones, like Bob Ross, who told us, “The only great work is to love what you do. And if you can’t love it, laugh at it!”

This is a regular sense of what we’ve done. Drop and stop Trump and add something to laugh about.

That was Thomas Jefferson’s line: “I find that the harder I work, the more luck I seem to have. Or maybe I’m just more easily amused.”

Again, the amusement is vital, especially having to deal with Trump.

To add two good ones to end this group, they started with Edward Bergen, “Hard work never killed anybody, but why take a chance?”

Then they ended with, “Success is not the key to happiness. Happiness is the key to success. So, if you’re happy, just pretend you’re successful!”

And to end it with a few funny leadership ideas: “When I talk to managers, I get the feeling that they are important. When I talk to leaders, I get the feeling that I am important” (Alexander den Heijer).

Then there was the question: “Who ought to be boss?” It was like asking, “Who ought to be the tenor in the quartet?” The answer was, “Obviously, the man who can sing tenor.”

 Tony Deyal and Gregory Wight agreed with John Naisbitt, “Leadership is the art of getting someone else to do something you want done because he wants to do it.” Send feedback to columns@gleanerjm.com

news.title: California Dems’ doomed ICE stunt rightfully shredded by judge
news.text:
California’s latest attempt to override the US Constitution in service of a radical left-wing agenda has just been thrown out by the federal courts.

This week, United States District Judge Christina A. Snyder issued a permanent injunction barring the state from enforcing two laws (SB 627 and 805) that would require Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to wear badges, and prevent them from wearing masks.

It is beyond obvious why ICE agents need those protections. The far left and its street militias will stop at nothing to stalk, harass, and attack anyone who works for ICE. Exposing the personal information of any ICE agent would put him or her in grave danger, and undermine the rule of law.

Democrats in Sacramento (notably Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, who introduced both laws) simply ignored these risks, and voted to put the men and women who protect our country in danger.

It was clear from the beginning that these laws were unconstitutional. They carved out an exception for the California Highway Patrol, which is unlawful discrimination against federal officers. Wiener introduced a new law (SB 1004) that purported to address that problem, but which still suffered from the fatal flaw of encroaching on immigration enforcement, which is an area of exclusive federal jurisdiction.

Democrats cannot have it both ways. They cannot demand that states like Arizona have no power to enforce federal immigration law, while also trying to use their supermajority in the California Legislature to direct ICE agents in their jobs.

California Democrats have a habit of passing laws that are unconstitutional on their face, simply to generate partisan propaganda and friendly media coverage. 

Perhaps the most ridiculous example came in 2024, when Gavin Newsom tried to ban the use of “deepfake” AI videos making fun of politicians like Kamala Harris. The federal judiciary tossed that law out at the earliest opportunity as a violation of the First Amendment. Today, Democrats freely use AI-generated videos for political purposes, and nobody seems bothered by it.

It is a disgrace that California and other Democrat-run states still refuse to allow federal officers to enforce bipartisan immigration law. They are following the poisonous precedent of the South in the era of slavery, when states claimed the power to nullify federal law. 

Like the Confederate heresy, Democrats’ perverse “sanctuary” philosophy will be judged by history for the grave affront to democracy that it really is.

news.title: Ahead of 2028, a presidential campaign is building behind AOC
news.text:
At the height of midterm hustings, Donald Trump made a peculiar comment about one of his fiercest critics in Congress.

"Somehow I don't mind AOC that much," the US president said at a Michigan rally, using Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's nickname. "I don't know why, she doesn't bug me too much."

It could have been a sign the dial has shifted on the Democratic representative, from firebrand progressive to an unlikely bridge between America's far left and the right.

And in the wake of the midterms' "bluenami", speculation that Ms Ocasio-Cortez is popular enough to be elected president has reached a fever pitch.

Almost a dozen Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapters, including in Chicago, Los Angeles, San Diego and Washington DC, have recently passed resolutions urging her to launch a 2028 campaign.

Separately, a political organisation called Ready for AOC launched earlier this month, aiming to gather at least a million signatures in support of a presidential run.

There are suggestions Ms Ocasio-Cortez would be a serious contender outside socialist ranks as well.

Just days before the midterms, an AtlasIntel poll asked blue voters who they would support in the party primaries for the 2028 election.

Ms Ocasio-Cortez ranked second, only a slim margin behind Georgia senator Jon Ossoff and 5 points higher than the party's last presidential candidate, Kamala Harris.

On Kalshi and Polymarket, America's two best-known betting markets - according to US political media outlet The Hill - she similarly has the second-highest odds next to Mr Ossoff.

From bartender to potential president

From the moment Ms Ocasio-Cortez entered politics — when she pulled off the biggest primary upset in 2018 to beat 10-term incumbent and Democratic Caucus chair Joe Crowley — there has been talk of her presidential potential.

At 29, the former bartender became the youngest woman and youngest Latina ever elected to Congress.

Only months later, an NBC News poll found three-quarters of Democratic and leaning-blue voters would consider voting for her to be president.

In the years since, she has become one of America's most followed politicians online, where her socialist-leaning policies of Medicare for all, stronger immigrant rights and affordable housing have drawn an audience of millions.

Ms Ocasio-Cortez has not yet said whether she will run for president in 2028, but her office released a memo touting her wide appeal after the Democrats' resounding midterms victory on November 3.

"Rep. Ocasio-Cortez has built a record of success that extends beyond her own electoral victories … [emerging] as one of the most powerful endorsements in the United States and New York State specifically," it read.

One of the achievements listed was her "race-changing endorsement" of fellow Democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani, who comfortably won the New York City mayoral race last year on promises of free childcare, free city buses and freezing rents.

It also highlighted how she held three major rallies and raised $US1 million ($1.48 million) in support for Abdul El-Sayed, whose victory in Michigan was one of the party's major midterm successes.

But the memo began with Ms Ocasio-Cortez's reflections after the 2024 presidential election when support for Mr Trump surged in her district of the Bronx.

Many of Ms Ocasio-Cortez's supporters split their tickets to vote for both her and Mr Trump, whose numbers in the largely Black, Asian and Latino district jumped 11 per cent.

At the same time, Ms Ocasio-Cortez was comfortably re-elected to a fourth term, securing almost 69 per cent of votes in the House race.

"There is universal frustration in this country, much of it I think justified, that is raging at a political establishment that centres corporate interests and billionaires and puts their needs ahead of the needs of working Americans," she said at the time, after reaching out to those voters.

AOC's reach over party divides

In the two years since, she has worked to position herself as a champion of the working class and a "kind of friendly neighbourhood lefty", according to The New York Times's Matt Flegenheimer, who said she evoked both "the people-over-profits populism of Bernie Sanders and the more-unites-than-divides-us appeals of Barack Obama".

As part of her evolution, Ms Ocasio-Cortez has met with Make America Healthy Again activists, where she has found common ground on issues like pesticides, and people in rural Georgia whose homes are now beside a massive Meta data centre.

In her comments about a potential presidential run, Ms Ocasio-Cortez has not shied away from the roadblocks in her path.

At the top of that list is the fact the United States has never elected a woman as president. Across Congress, men outnumber women almost three to one.

"Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ms Ocasio-Cortez told The New York Times in September.

In the same interview, Ms Ocasio-Cortez said some people had suggested 2028 may be her "political window".

"Oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot … life doesn't wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you," she said.

Is the US ready for a progressive president?

The speculation comes as the Democratic Party turns to internal battles, with some cautioning against leaning too far left and others seeing the midterm results as an endorsement of progressive policies.

There are also suggestions Ms Ocasio-Cortez will run for the Senate instead, as New York Democrat Chuck Schumer is up for re-election in 2028 and has not yet said whether he plans to run.

Doug Sosnik, a senior advisor to former president Bill Clinton, described Ms Ocasio-Cortez as an "unbelievable political talent" who has "the Zeitgeist of our times" at her fingertips.

But he questioned whether her appeal could extend beyond the Democratic base.

"I think she would be an extremely powerful force in the Democratic primary," Mr Sosnik told AP.

Others, including in Republican circles, have taken a more positive view.

Andrew Kolvet, executive producer of The Charlie Kirk Show and a spokesperson for Turning Point USA, said Ms Ocasio-Cortez was seen as "a Democrat with game".

"AOC and Mamdani, yes, they have awful policies and ideas, but they are inarguably the best raw political talents of the far left," he said.

DSA spokesperson Cara Tobe said the Democrats' overwhelming success at the midterms "would not have been possible without a socialist surge".

"People are starting to realise and learn that socialism is not a big scary word," she told AP.

"The big thing is people are looking for change. This is actually part of what even led Trump to victory."
news.summary: In the wake of the midterms' "bluenami", speculation that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is popular enough to be elected America's first female president has reached a fever pitch.

news.title: The 2026 midterms on Kalshi and Polymarket - Pew Research Center
news.text:
Prediction markets saw $2.7 billion in trading related to this year’s midterm elections in the United States, according to a Pew Research Center analysis of data from The Block, a digital assets media and information firm.

Trading volume on this year’s elections pales in comparison to the $8.5 billion traded on the 2024 elections, the majority of which was on the presidential race. It’s also below the amount traded so far on the upcoming 2028 presidential election. Questions like who will win each party’s nomination and which candidate will win the general election in 2028 have already drawn $3 billion in trading volume.

The two major prediction markets included in this analysis, Kalshi and Polymarket, have promoted their election event contracts as tools for accurately forecasting the races. They’ve also reported that many users visit their sites for information without placing trades. Some news sites have used prediction market odds in their election reporting.

Critics of election-related trading have raised concerns about election integrity, including insider trading and manipulating the odds on low-volume markets. More than half of states restrict betting on elections, but prediction markets are not currently regulated as gambling operators.

How has election-related trading evolved in recent years?

In 2024, nearly all election-related trading was focused on the presidential election. The markets on whether Donald Trump or Kamala Harris would win the election still rank as two of the three highest-volume markets of all time, political or otherwise, on both Kalshi and Polymarket. (On Kalshi, the first is related to who would win the 2026 FIFA World Cup.)

In 2025, off-cycle trading was similarly dominated by a single campaign: the New York City mayoral election. Three-quarters of election trading volume in 2025 pertained to that race, with more than a quarter of it spent on markets that mentioned Zohran Mamdani, the winning candidate, by name.

In 2026, trading volume was more dispersed across a range of races: 70% of trading volume focused on control of Congress or individual congressional elections, and nearly a quarter was devoted to gubernatorial elections. Other state and local races made up the rest.

Which races were traded most heavily in 2026?

In 2026, two-thirds of election trading volume was on markets that mentioned individual states, up from just 15% in 2024.

Statewide races for Senate and governor are usually the marquee elections in midterm years. Many of the races with the highest trading volume this year were high-profile, competitive Senate contests like those in Texas, Michigan and Maine.

Notably, 42% of total election-related trading volume in 2026 — over $1 billion — was on races in states where election betting is illegal in at least some instances. Some states warned voters that prediction markets’ election contracts violate those laws.

How many election-related markets existed in 2026?

Although the amount of money traded on election markets was lower this year than in 2024, the number of markets available to trade was far higher. In 2026, users traded on around 34,000 election-related markets on Kalshi and Polymarket, up from about 2,300 in 2024.

Many of the markets related to the 2026 midterms were “thinly traded” – that is, low-volume ones where relatively small amounts of money could meaningfully change the odds. Nearly half of all election markets in 2026 had less than $1,000 in trading volume, compared with just 4% in 2024.

Conversely, a small number of popular markets saw the vast majority of trading volume in 2026. Some 90% of election-related trading volume in 2026 went to 1,087 markets – only around 3% of the total number of available markets.

Markets with no trading volume are excluded from all calculations in this section, such as the number and share of available markets.

How does political trading differ between Kalshi and Polymarket?

Politics makes up a relatively small share of overall trading volume on Kalshi and Polymarket, which have come to be dominated by sports.

While both platforms saw a marked increase in political trading the week of the midterms, politics remains a much higher-volume trading topic on Polymarket than on Kalshi.

The two platforms also differ in the type of political questions that traders focus on:

On Kalshi, 72% of political trading since 2024 has been related to U.S. elections. The rest pertained to elections outside the U.S. or other political topics like legislative developments or the behavior of elected officials.

On Polymarket, those other questions dominate. Just 35% of political trading volume since 2024 was related to U.S. elections.

news.title: 'The View' co-host stunned as Hostin backs Gavin Newsom bypassing victims' families for death row commutations
news.text: "The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeared surprised when co-host Sunny Hostin disagreed with her argument that Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom should have notified the victims' families before ending the death sentences of 548 inmates in his state. "I don’t like the way it went through. And I think that before he announced that, he needed to get the approval and agreement of the families of the victims, because the people that he’s commuted the sentences for are people who are on death row. They’re people who committed murder, and I tend to be against blanket pardon to begin with," Navarro said. Newsom commuted the death sentences of all of California's death-row inmates in early November, effectively ending capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions. CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE' "I think these are things you have to take on a case-by-case basis, and I think it’s disrespectful to the victims’ families," Navarro said. "You can disagree or agree with the death penalty, but to me, if your loved one has been murdered, you have the right to be told that this is happening, before you read about it." Hostin said, "I disagree with that." "That the victim's family should have been told?" Navarro asked in response. "Yes," Hostin repeated. "I'm an opponent of the death penalty. I think that God gives life." Hostin said those cases were under Newsom's purview as governor. She argued that the system is "broken," and no one should have to pay the ultimate price for a broken system. ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION "One innocent person being put to death is not worth the entire system," she said. "And if you look at the system, it's not a deterrent. That the statistics show that more than half of death row exonerees are Black, even though Black people just make up 13.6% of the U.S. population. "And nearly 60% of the people that are found to have been wrongfully convicted of murder by the Innocence Project are African Americans, and so the system is broken," Hostin continued. "And you should not pay the ultimate price for a system that is broken." Co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin sided with Navarro, arguing the move was a betrayal of the families. "It was a betrayal of the families to not notify them beforehand," Griffin said. "People can agree or disagree on the death penalty. It's actually come up as a ballot initiative in California twice in the last decade. And California voters actually voted to keep capital punishment in place. "I think (Newsom) has the purview to do this, but then to not notify families, that gets in the way of their grief," she added. "There's no greater trauma than having a loved one murdered in a brutal way and thinking it's been adjudicated in the court, and there's a certain outcome in finding out in a newspaper, basically, that that's not happening." GAVIN NEWSOM SEEKS COUNSEL FROM ‘MASTER’ BILL CLINTON AS HE PLOTS PROJECT 2029 Griffin also said it could be a political move by Newsom. "This should have been handled better," she said. "And I think there's a political side to this too. He wants to run for president. He wants to seem more progressive. Kamala Harris may run for president. He's gonna be like, ‘She was a prosecutor who put people in jail.’ So, I don't like it. He should have notified the families." Co-host Sara Haines agreed, arguing that undoing all the death sentences treated each case the same. "I think the point is that if you want to change something going forward, put it on a ballot, and clearly California doesn't want it taken off," she said. "At that point, I think he should have looked case-by-case, because to not reach out to these families, they get nothing back. "Any closure they get is small. But some of these people deeply found something in this conviction and this determination. And to just undo it in one blanket swipe is to treat them all the same." When reached for comment, the governor's office referred Fox News Digital to a letter Newsom issued explaining his decision. In part, Newsom wrote, "This decision is among the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims' families. I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss. "I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action," he continued. "Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing." Later in the letter, Newsom said, "California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books, and I respect that. I recognize the limits of this clemency action, which does not repeal the death penalty and is limited to commuting California's current death sentences. The power to repeal the death penalty rests with the Legislature and voters." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "Victims’ rights were disregarded and trampled by Governor Newsom," Y. David Scharf, chairman of Morrison Cohen LLP, told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Whatever one’s view of the death penalty, the families of murder victims deserved more than to learn that the sentences in their loved ones’ cases were being swept away as part of a blanket decision affecting hundreds of cases. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The governor may have the constitutional authority to commute these sentences, but having the power to do something does not mean the people most profoundly affected by it should be treated as an afterthought," he continued. "At a minimum, these families deserved notice, respect and an opportunity to be heard before such a consequential decision was announced."
news.summary: Sunny Hostin and Ana Navarro were split over Newsom's 548 death row commutations, and Navarro argued that Gov. Gavin Newsom should have notified the families.

news.title: Black Voters Swung the South. Their Message to Democrats: Don’t Squander This.
news.text:
After a slew of historic firsts on November 3, including the election of the first Black woman governor in US history, Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms, the internet was flooded with posts crediting Stacey Abrams, the first Black woman to run for governor on a major-party ticket, with helping make Democrats’ big wins in the South possible. 

About a week later, Abrams received her flowers for real at Facing Race, the country’s largest multiracial racial justice conference, in Raleigh, North Carolina. At the center of Facing Race was people power—and what to do with it next.

On Thursday—the day after Senator-elect Scott Colom was declared the winner of a race that will make him Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction—thousands of community organizers, public servants, artists, and activists gathered for three days in the home of the South’s oldest historically Black college, Shaw University, birthplace of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee.

The mood in Raleigh was celebratory yet cautious, as racial justice practitioners took stock of their hard-fought victories while preparing for the battles ahead, including the need for ongoing resistance to authoritarianism and greater political investment in the South.

“I ended up being extremely proud of what we were able to see in Alabama and especially across the South,” said Tamela Glover, a 39-year-old native of Selma and organizer with the nonprofit Alabama Rise. In Glover’s home state, House Rep. Shomari Figures was resoundingly reelected in a district that the state GOP redrew to try and oust him. “But I also know that we can’t just celebrate. The real work begins with holding everybody accountable.”

Facing Race’s location and theme—“rooted in resistance, powered by solidarity”—were chosen long before Democrats flipped North Carolina’s state House and ended a GOP supermajority in the state Senate, former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper flipped an open Senate seat, and Democrats flipped several House seats redistricted to favor Republicans: a map drawn to secure Republicans an 11-3 split in North Carolina’s House delegation is now poised to end up 11-3 for Democrats.

“It’s great to celebrate the wins we saw,” said Glenn Harris, the president of Race Forward, the nonprofit that organizes Facing Race. “But the thing that we can always celebrate is the history of Black organizing in this country.”

“Using North Carolina as an example,” Harris said, “that was not just about what’s happening in the political moment. That was about years of building statewide infrastructure that allowed folks to take advantage of that moment.”

Friday kicked off with a keynote address by Abrams, who briefly outlined her rise to national prominence: beginning in 2018, when she narrowly lost the Georgia gubernatorial race to then–Georgia Secretary of State Brian Kemp, whom President Trump later repudiated for refusing to help him rig Georgia’s 2020 election results. The same year, Abrams founded Fair Fight Action, a nonprofit dedicated to fighting voter suppression—a practice her opponent had been accused of by multiple civil rights groups in a 2018 lawsuit. Abrams and Kemp faced off again in 2022. Abrams has since launched numerous other initiatives to fight authoritarianism and protect diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. (“I’m basically the Costco of democracy,” Abrams said during her keynote.)

A couple of days before Facing Race, Abrams published a Substack newsletter titled “After the Wave, the Work,” in which she noted that despite Democrats’ new majorities in both chambers of Congress, Republicans still controlled the executive and judicial branches. We’re “living through,” Abrams wrote, what political scientists Steve Levitsky and Lucan Way call “competitive authoritarianism,” where certain components of democracy like elections continue imperfectly while the party in power exploits and redraws the government’s institutions in their favor. 

In her keynote address on Friday, Abrams laid out a ten-step framework for understanding how authoritarianism occurs and characterized the current “moment of opportunity” as a “time where people have been so angry that they could not keep their voices contained, where they were so outraged by the outrage of the Supreme Court to strip us of our voting rights that they showed up anyway.”

Spurred by the Supreme Court’s erosion of the Voting Rights Act in April’s Louisiana v. Callais decision, which gave the go-ahead for GOP-controlled legislatures to gerrymander majority-Black districts in the South out of existence, droves of Black voters showed up to the ballot box and voted overwhelmingly for Democrats.

“They proved that participation does not eliminate discrimination,” Abrams said. “But they were never going to let it stop them from having the patience and the perseverance to make change.”

According to the Nationhood Lab, a project of Salve Regina University’s Pell Center, CNN exit polls showed democracy was a top voter concern—behind only the economy—in Georgia, South Carolina, Mississippi, and Florida, where Democrats made significant gains.

In my conversations with the people attending Facing Race—from the Deep South; to the nation’s capital, which just elected its first democratic socialist mayor; to Midwestern cities that were the sites of aggressive ICE operations and powerful resistance—all emphasized that they saw the midterm victories as merely a starting point for defending democracy. 

Andrea Pérez-Maikkula, a 43-year-old DEI practitioner born in Puerto Rico and living in Minnesota, said she was excited about the blue wave, especially Peggy Flanagan’s Minnesota Senate win, making Flanagan the first Native American woman to secure election to the upper chamber. 

But Pérez-Maikkula is also “concerned about what’s going to happen when the excitement dies down,” adding, “If we just stay complacent with the results alone, we’re not going to be in a good place a couple of years from now.”

Another consensus was that Democrats could have won even bigger prizes had they invested more in races in the South previously considered long shots. 

Cultural critic, sociologist, and University of North Carolina Center for Information, Technology and Public Life professor Tressie McMillan Cottom, another keynote speaker, challenged the prevailing assumption in the media and in national Democratic circles that rural means white. According to a Politico analysis of initial election data, majority Black counties in the South saw “the greatest surges in turnout this cycle compared to the 2022 midterms.”

Cottom also spoke about Democrats’ neglect of the South, naming Florida—where state Rep. Angie Nixon, the Democratic Senate nominee, lost by less than three percentage points to Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody—as a prime example of a lost opportunity for Democrats.

“People are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South,” Nixon herself told MS NOW weeks before the midterms, arguing that Florida isn’t a “red state; it is an underinvested state.”

Nixon won the state’s most populous county, Miami-Dade, by more than seven points, defying all expectations for a self-proclaimed democratic socialist in a place where the label “communist”—which has more negative resonance in Miami than perhaps anywhere else in the country—was relentlessly weaponized against her. (Then–Vice President Kamala Harris lost Miami-Dade in 2024 by more than one and a half times that margin.) Nixon has suggested that she’ll run again in 2028.

Up until the week before the election, Black and Latino lawmakers, and their allies, were arguing that they needed more funding from the national party. While the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Senate Majority PAC poured large sums of money into competitive races in other parts of the country, critics said their funding of Senate candidates in the South was too little, too late. 

The Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates, reportedly gave $150 million to Sherrod Brown in Ohio, $67 million to Josh Turek in Iowa, and the same amount to Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan—after Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer and the establishment initially hesitated to embrace him; $65 million to Troy Jackson in Maine; and tens of millions more for races in Texas and Kansas. 

But Colom received just $2.2 million from SMP for Mississippi, and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews just $750,000. Nixon, in Florida, and Jamie Davis in Louisiana—who both ran stunningly close Senate races in Republican strongholds—seemingly went without any direct funding at all.

Davis, like Colom, would have become his state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction; he lost by less than two points.

Just days after his win, Colom—whose national funding mainly consisted of a modest last-minute injection of ad money—told NBC’s Meet the Press: “In the South, we had to do more with less. In Mississippi, we got it out the mud,” adding that “what we need to do now as a Democratic Party is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment.”

As Adam Mahoney of Capital B pointed out, some of the country’s closest Senate races were those in Louisiana, Florida, Mississippi, and South Carolina, where the Democratic establishment spent significantly less on advertising than in other races.

The ongoing work of building multiracial democracy came up again and again; Abrams emphasized it towards the end of her speech with an impassioned call for attendees to hold their newly elected officials to account.

“We’ve got to start showing up in their offices and reminding them of their intention,” Abrams said. “We’ve got to write bills for them and make sure we find voters for them. We’ve got to find the power and the confidence for them. We’ve got to find them courage while we’re at it, because they are going to start to believe that these seats are theirs and not yours.”
