news.title: ‘SNL’ ‘Sister’ sketch nails the failures of US healthcare policy
news.text:
A “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “Sister” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free?

The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families.

According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women.

As researchers who study aging, long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts.

While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide.

Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care

One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities.

Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit, limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements.

This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025.

For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends.

Medicaid can help, but access is limited

Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer.

Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023. The divide between these programs dates back to 1965, when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew.

However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance.

Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services.

Who provides care in the meantime?

There’s a shortage of paid caregivers

Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle.

The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born.

The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025, only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned. 

Caregiving often has financial consequences

When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care.

Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out.

Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks.

Families often have to shoulder responsibility

Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states, for example, have launched paid family leave programs. In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers. Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage.

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance, an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election.

“Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place.

When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter.
news.summary: Medicare and Medicaid provide limited help with caregiving for older adults – and that means unpaid relatives often bear big burdens.

news.title: Longtime Trump Pal Says He’s ‘Embarrassed’ by ‘Pathetic’ President
news.text:
On CNN’s NewsNight, host Audie Cornish asked Rivera about Trump’s effusive friendliness towards authoritarian leaders Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. 

“I think that if they’re friends, why doesn’t Trump ask his friend to stop bombing hospitals, to stop bombing daycare centers, to stop bombing civilian homes, to stop bombing civilian infrastructure, energy infrastructure, so they’re gonna freeze — the Ukrainians are gonna freeze,” said Rivera. “It’s just pathetic. I was embarrassed for the president.”

Rivera and Trump’s friendship goes back to the 1970s, yet after the January 6, 2021, Capitol riots, he broke with the president and voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024. 

On Thursday’s show, Rivera also asked what Trump had achieved during his trip to China, adding: “What was it about? It was a three-day junket, what? To walk down the red carpet?” 

He also clashed with fellow panelist conservative pundit Jason Rantz, who argued that Trump was trying to cover “all sorts of topics” in discussions with the leaders and was trying to forge a relationship with Putin to serve long-term goals. 

Rivera hit back at Trump’s apparent lack of a negotiating strategy, arguing: “You go in with a pre-prepared agreement that people have to negotiate.

“You talk about the friendship that Trump forges with Putin, and you say eight months later, Putin invades Ukraine. So what the hell is this friendship about? What’s the friendship about when all of these hundreds of thousands of people are being killed?”

Trump has faced harsh criticism in the wake of the summit, where he took part in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., Russia, and China. 

The president lavished the two strongmen with praise, yet left the summit with no concrete diplomatic victories in areas including nuclear weapons control, the war in Ukraine, and AI. 

Among the key items Trump discussed with Putin was the Ukraine war, which has left millions dead and which Trump has long pledged to bring an end to. 

In the last few months, Russia has escalated brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilian targets and infrastructure. 

Yet after discussions with Trump, Putin ruled out a ceasefire, instead saying that Russia would seek revenge for a Ukrainian strike that destroyed a section of the Crimea Bridge.

Rivera defended Trump during his first presidential run in 2016, though he later said he didn’t vote for him. In the wake of the Capitol riot, he called for the president’s impeachment, saying he “unleashed a mob to make war on their own government.”

news.title: The Patriot Post® · 2028 Is Looking Like 2016 but Upside Down
news.text:
The two parties’ presidential lineups look a lot like those of the 2015-16 cycle — in reverse.

Republicans emerged from the 2014 midterm elections with large congressional majorities (247 House members and 54 senators). Democrats have emerged from this year’s midterm elections with even larger ones (259 House members and 56 senators).

But Democrats then, like Republicans now, had a much smaller field of prospective presidential candidates. Two figures in former President Barack Obama’s party towered over the others in visibility and popularity — his vice president, Joe Biden, and his first-term secretary of state, Hillary Clinton.

Recent vice presidents had won the presidency or come close, among them Richard Nixon, Hubert Humphrey, George H.W. Bush and Al Gore. No former secretary of state had won the presidency since James Buchanan in 1856. Yet Obama favored Clinton over Biden.

One reason may have been age. Clinton would have been 69 at the outset of the next presidential term, while Biden would have been 74. That didn’t prevent Biden from becoming the consensus choice for the nomination four years later. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who was 75 by the next inauguration, was even older. He entered the primaries from stage left, winning 22 primaries and caucuses and holding Clinton to a 55%-43% advantage in votes cast for the nomination.

Today’s Republican field looks as small as the Democratic field did at the same point in that cycle. It, too, includes a vice president and a secretary of state, with room for a third candidate who is no one’s idea of a Washington insider.

Vice President JD Vance is in his first term, while Biden was in his second, and Vance’s two years in the Senate pale beside Biden’s 36. But Vance has the advantage of youth. He will be just 44 on Inauguration Day in 2029. Like Clinton, Secretary of State Marco Rubio served in the Senate — 14 years in his case, eight in hers. If elected in 2028, he would take the presidential oath at the mature but hardly elderly age of 57.

Rubio’s statement that he won’t run if Vance does can be read as an attempt to avoid turmoil in the Trump administration — a predictably unattainable goal. In the two weeks since the election, Vance has attributed the Republican rout solely to military action against Iran, which Rubio has supported. President Donald Trump, in turn, has publicly ordered Vance to give his full attention to exposing Democratic corruption in large cities.

Trump’s favor may shift, and it may count for less than it once did. The Republican polling firm Echelon Insights reports that 56% of Republicans see themselves as party-first and only 36% as Trump-first. Another 51% say it is time to “move beyond the Trump approach.”

The RealClearPolitics average of seven polls on the Republican nomination this fall shows Vance leading Rubio by a less-than-overwhelming margin, 37% to 28%. Outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-Fla.) draws 10%.

DeSantis’ record of policy success in Florida, the only one of the 10 largest states to remain safely Republican this year, could make him a serious contender. He would be just 50 on Inauguration Day in 2029.

Meanwhile, Democrats, still giddy over their success, could field as many presidential candidates as the 10 Republicans who competed in the 2016 caucuses and primaries. That Republican field included senators from Florida, Kentucky and Texas; current and former governors from Arkansas, Florida, New Jersey and Ohio; a pediatric surgeon from Maryland; a former tech CEO from California; and a real estate developer and reality TV host from New York.

Trump won that crowded contest despite taking positions on trade, war and economic policy far outside those of previous Republican presidents. By the time he won an outright majority in any state, 36 states had already voted.

The Democratic field now taking shape looks something like that Republican field. The RealClearPolitics average of recent polls shows measurable support for 10 candidates. They include governors from California, Illinois, Kentucky and Pennsylvania, senators from Arizona, Georgia and New Jersey, a House member from New York, a former transportation secretary, and former Vice President Kamala Harris, the party’s 2024 nominee.

They range widely in age and experience. If Harris took the presidential oath in January 2029, she would be the eighth-oldest person to do so for the first time. Just days would separate her from Zachary Taylor and George H.W. Bush. Only William Henry Harrison, Buchanan, Ronald Reagan, Trump and Biden were older than all three when they first took office. At the other end of the list, either Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), at 41, or Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), at 39, would be the youngest president ever.

The field could grow or shrink. Someone whose candidacy seems as improbable as Trump’s did a dozen years ago could enter the race and win.

America’s two political parties have retained their basic characters across centuries. The Republican Party has always centered on people who see themselves, and whom others see, as typical Americans. In a nation that has always been culturally diverse, they have never made up a majority on their own.

The Democratic Party has always been a coalition of outsiders, people who see themselves, and whom others see, as outside the American mainstream. If they hold together, they can form a majority.

When Democrats lack a dominant leader — and Obama, nearly 10 years out of office, no longer seems to play that role — the danger is that the party’s disparate constituencies will extract concessions that help candidates win the nomination but cost them votes in the general election.

Transgender advocates’ demand for sex-change surgery for prisoners, which Harris docilely endorsed on camera, wounded her candidacy in 2024, perhaps fatally. Other demands from the period Ocasio-Cortez called “Woke 1” included defunding the police, admitting all otherwise illegal immigrants who claim asylum, allowing biological men in girls’ sports and women’s prisons, and requiring masks during the COVID-19 pandemic. Endorsing such demands may help candidates win support in the spring 2028 primaries but prove disastrous in the general election.

Democrats will have a hard time balancing public demands for “affordability” with calls for more public spending from teachers unions and victims’ groups. Continued demands for racial quotas and preferences in hiring and political districting may also seem beside the point. The country elected a Black president in 2008, and voters just elected a Black Democratic senator in Mississippi and a Black Republican governor in Florida.

In days of yore, local Democratic bosses could grant concessions on some issues and mollify those whose demands they rejected. Today, the very existence of single-issue groups — and their payrolls — depends on wresting concessions from the party on unpopular issues. Popular positions usually don’t need paid advocates.

As analysts have noted, most voters in the electorate that gave Democrats large majorities still view the party unfavorably. In the midterm elections, voters could use Democrats as a check on an increasingly disconnected Trump without giving the party full control of the government. In 2028, Democrats will ask for just that, while voters will likely see little risk of Republicans winning the presidency and both chambers of Congress, as they did in 2016 and 2024.

That’s why Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston, who have been giving Democrats good advice for more than 30 years, write that “the midterms say little about who will win in 2028” and “do not conclusively show which kind of Democrat would be more electable at the national level in 2028.”

Democrats are fortunate that their majorities are large enough to limit the leverage of the Democratic Socialists of America and other leftists in setting policy. But the left has a cheering section in the press and among affluent college graduates, who lately have been the party’s largest constituency. Both groups will likely push the party leftward.

None of this is set in stone. Choices yet to be made and events yet to occur will shape the outcome, as they did 10 years ago. Democrats have an opportunity to present an attractive face, but they have flubbed such opportunities before. Republicans, for all their drubbing this year, still have assets that Trump, busy redesigning the White House complex and cleaning the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, has left undeployed.

news.title: As Kamala Harris mulls 2028, some Democrats are ready to move on
news.text:
WASHINGTON – With the midterms behind them, Democrats are turning to the 2028 presidential race and wondering what the party's most recent nominee, former Vice President Kamala Harris, will do.

Harris is a frontrunner in surveys and near universally known among Democrats after her unsuccessful bid for the White House in 2024. But she hasn't said what her plans are — and more than two dozen other politicians in her party are looking at potential runs. The list includes Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Prominent Democrats, potential political staffers and voters are already sizing up the expected candidates. And they say Harris' decision will define the campaign that's expected to begin in earnest as soon as next month.

Harris 2028? Kamala Harris says she won't run for California governor

"I’ve publicly encouraged other candidates that are thinking about it, now that the midterms are over to at least respect her timeline," civil rights leader and National Action Network founder Al Sharpton said. "Of course, if it goes too long, I understand that. But right now, in this period, if I were one running, I would consider what she's going to do and respect that."

Sharpton, whose endorsement is highly sought among Democrats running for president, said other candidates have the right to challenge the former vice president. But he said they should let Harris, who received more than 75 million votes in 2024, make her decision first and know with certainty that they'd be going up against her.

It's a request that many, in what could be an extremely crowded field, are not likely to follow. Anticipated contenders include two governors whose terms are ending in January, at least one House member and several former officeholders.

In conversations with more than a dozen Harris allies, party strategists and progressive leaders, Democrats said they viewed Harris as having the longest amount of time compared to her competitors to make a decision of anyone in the potential field. Several said she could wait until the first primary debate to make an announcement if she wanted.

But that doesn’t mean she should, they argued. Other expected candidates are making plays for endorsements, donors and campaign staff, with some saying publicly that their timelines won't be affected by anyone else.

"I think people are going to announce when they want to announce," said Meghan Hays, who was a senior aide to former President Joe Biden. "I don't think they're factoring her in at all."

Democrats considering 2028 bids have already started to collect resumes for potential campaign staff, two people told USA TODAY. One of the people described them as governors. Two people familiar with the conversations taking place around 2028 said that at least two candidates were toying with December announcements.

Candidates who aren’t as well known as the former vice president may want to start courting voters in early-voting states and raising money sooner rather than later, leading Democrats say. Others will decide to save their money and resources and announce at the beginning of the second fundraising quarter.

"It's about what kind of operation people are going to build," said South Carolina Democratic Party chair Christale Spain, who was the state director for New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker during his presidential bid. "The runway is what it is. You don't get any more days."

Harris was undecided on another presidential bid heading into the November midterm elections, three people familiar with her thinking told USA TODAY, but she has taken steps to keep the door open, campaigning in a string of states last month and reconnecting with donors, as she raised funds for her leadership PAC.

She has sent multiple fundraising emails to grassroots supporters since then that talk up the upcoming Democratic majority without addressing her own potential ambitions.

"I know that these midterm elections were not easy. It has been a challenging couple of years. Now, we can move forward together to deliver the change we need," Harris said in a Nov. 8 message.

'107 Days': Kamala Harris says 'recklessness' drove silence on Biden in 2024 campaign

Democrats are moving on

Former South Carolina lawmaker Bakari Sellers was a cochair in 2019 of Harris' campaign in his home state. But he has not talked to Harris in awhile and said she has work to do.

He's been to church with Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and hung out with California Rep. Ro Khanna. He's had Moore, of Maryland, and Buttigieg, a former South Bend, Indiana, mayor, over to his house.

Sellers said he has an open door policy and thinks of many of the expected candidates as friends.

Harris is the best known of the potential candidates, but she has to reassure Democrats who don't think a woman or a Black person can win, Sellers said, and demonstrate she can hire a team that can get her to the White House.

"She's more Hillary Clinton '08 than Barack Obama, but you choose your fighter," said Sellers, whose home state hosts the first Democratic primary in 2028.

Clinton, a former first lady and sitting U.S. senator, lost the primary in 2008 to Obama, who'd only been in Washington for two years when he announced his presidential bid. He went on to win the general election and serve two terms as president.

Potential rival: Josh Shapiro dishes on Harris VP search, Biden and Trump in new book

Harris lands among the frontrunners in polling, but she's not alone. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released this month found that 23% of Democratic voters said they believed Harris would be an "excellent" candidate, compared to 29% who said the same of Buttigieg and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff.

Other recent polls have shown Harris either leading the presumptive field or among the top picks of those surveyed.

An Emerson College poll released Nov. 19 showed Ossoff leading the field among self-identified primary voters with 17% support. He was followed by Ocasio-Cortez at 12%, Newsom at 8%, Buttigieg at 6%, Harris at 6%, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear with 4% and Kelly at 3%.

Regardless of what Harris decides to do, Democrats familiar with the conversations that are underway, say they’re expecting one of the largest primary fields in the party’s history.

"It's an open seat," Spain said. "And folks are going to take their chances."

Multiple potential Democratic candidates have laid out their own timelines to make a decision that have nothing to do with Harris.

Another Californian: Voters are frustrated with Biden over Gaza. Can Ro Khanna steer them back?

Khanna said he would decide after the December holidays. Beshear said he's "trying not to rush" into a decision and will talk to his teenage children. Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego recently told reporters he needs to figure out if he can balance his responsibilities as a father to young children with a presidential run.

Newsom, who leaves office Jan. 4, has said he'll make his decision at the beginning of the year. Newsom told CNN in September that he won't run if Harris does, saying that both Bay Area Democrats competing for the nomination would be "mutual assured destruction."

Sharpton said that he'd advise potential candidates to decide by Martin Luther King Jr. Day, which is observed annually in late January. "And I think that's reasonable to say that that is not preempting whatever decision she would make," Sharpton said of Harris.

Though Harris' situation is unique, as the party’s most recent nominee, there’s precedent for challenging a former Democratic vice president. It's one that Harris herself helped set in 2019 when she announced her bid on MLK Day amid a not so dissimilar dynamic.

At the time Biden, a two-time presidential candidate who decided against a 2016 bid after the death of his son, was known to be considering a third run. He waited until until April of that year to announce. Some Democrats say Harris can wait that long, as well, or until late spring when the first Democratic primary debate is expected to be held.

Harris courts voters, donors in midterms

A chief argument against Harris is that she's already competed for the presidency twice.

Her 2019 bid ended before any votes were cast, amid low polling and fundraising. In 2024, she quickly became her party’s nominee after Biden withdrew from the race less than four months before the general election. After a brief campaign, Harris lost every battleground state to President Donald Trump.

Harris' allies have bristled at any suggestion that she wouldn’t be a formidable primary opponent if she decides to run. One said people have underestimated how many voters have come in contact with the former vice president in the last two years.

The person pointed to Harris' seven-month book tour to promote her 2024 presidential election memoir, "107 Days," and requests she received to appear alongside Democratic candidates in tight races, including Sen.-elect Scott Colom in Mississippi and Gov.-elect David Crowley in Wisconsin.

Sharpton said he'd spoken to Harris several times about a potential run since she told him at the National Action Network Conference during an on-stage interview in April that she was considering one.

"She's still not made a final decision, but she has said that everywhere she goes, people are encouraging her to run," Sharpton, an MSNOW host, said in an interview.

Will Harris actually run?

Several factors appeared to be weighing on Harris' decision-making, including the outcome of the midterms, Sharpton said.

"I think she wants to see who may or may not be also considering and whether she could also, as much as possible, see who's going to be on the Republican side and assess if she feels that she has a better chance of succeeding against whomever the Republicans put up and whoever else is in the prospective field," the civil rights leader said.

A spokesperson for Harris did not respond to a request for comment.

Stephanie Valencia, cofounder of Equis Research and an outside adviser in 2024 to the Harris campaign on Latino outreach, said it's smart for the former vice president to be introspective and dig into the 2026 results, changes in the coalition and the potential for states like Texas to become battlegrounds.

Harris and other candidates must also consider the personal aspect, said Addisu Demissie, a Democratic strategist who managed Booker's 2020 presidential campaign. Demissie said he told Booker that running for president is a 10 year commitment – two years of campaigning and potentially eight years in office.

"Not to mention, it'll change your life forever if you win, or if you lose, so you have to decide if it's something you want to put yourself through, you want to put your family through," he told USA TODAY. "Just because she answered that question in the affirmative in 2018, and I guess it kind of was foisted upon her in 2024, doesn't mean she's necessarily going to answer it the same way now."

Some of Harris' previous backers are skeptical she’ll ultimately make a third attempt at the presidency. Sellers put it at 50-50.

Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic strategist and podcast host who writes a newsletter tracking the 2028 candidates, said he supported Harris when she ran for president in 2019, but he doesn’t believe she’ll launch another national campaign.

"I think she resents the fact that she's not considered an important voice in the party, and she should be," said Lehrich, who hosts a podcast with Harris' former deputy campaign manager. "That being said, I think people want to move on from 2024."

If she decides not to do it, Valencia said Harris — a former U.S. senator and California attorney general — would be an asset to 2028 contenders, who can learn from her experience in the White House and on the campaign trail.

"I don't think she should be just completely disregarded if she doesn't run," Valencia said. "I think there’s a lot she can add to the conversation. I think that she can also help to support and be a king or queen maker to whoever is seeking her support in 2028."

news.title: Republicans have a clear new frontrunner for 2028 – and it’s not Vance
news.text:
Vice President JD Vance is no longer the frontrunner to be the Republican Party’s nominee for the 2028 presidential race, according to a surprise new poll.

Vance was quick to acknowledge the blue wave that wiped out the GOP’s candidates at the midterms earlier this month, handing the majorities in both chambers of Congress to rival Democrats, and took to X to state plainly that the Iran war was the reason for his side’s loss. 

However, in a new post-election survey from Emerson Polling, the VP appears to be struggling to persuade voters he is the man to lead their party once President Donald Trump departs the scene, finishing second and picking up the support of just 20 percent of respondents.

Way out in front was Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who scored 36 percent of the vote – a major concern for Vance given that he led Rubio by 54 percent to six percent in the same poll just a year ago.

Although Vance is known to have opposed the Operation Epic Fury strikes against Tehran behind the scenes, he vowed to support Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in prosecuting the war and has not managed to escape association with it as one of the administration’s leading personalities.

Rubio, by contrast, has kept himself above the fray and busy with diplomatic missions around the world, cutting a serious and statesmanlike figure compared to some of his Cabinet colleagues.

The secretary joined Trump on his tour to Asia this week and delivered a no-nonsense press conference in Manila at which he confidently dismissed intelligence sector warnings about the prospect of Iran detonating a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C., and struck a soothing note on the recent spate of tech outages that have alarmed the public. 

By contrast, Vance joked on Fox News that it was not yet time for Americans to stockpile food and water or “build a bunker” and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin raised eyebrows by declaring “a guy that’s very smart with tech” had told him AI could be behind the outages. 

Rubio has previously said he would not challenge for the GOP nomination if Vance were also running out of loyalty to his friend – and got angry when he was asked about it recently – but the VP has yet to make any commitment and Trump has enjoyed asking aides which of the two men they prefer.

 Other candidates pitched in the Emerson poll drew a much less favorable response, with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis scoring seven percent, political novice Donald Trump Jr six percent and right-wing broadcaster Tucker Carlson five percent.

Vance’s potential candidacy received a further knock this week when another conservative influencer, Ben Shapiro, baldly stated that he should not be their party’s nominee in two years’ time.

“I think he’s extraordinarily online,” Shapiro said of the VP. “I think the vice president spends an inordinate amount of time worrying what the podcast bros think, like the Tucker Carlsons, and I think that he steers directly into that. 

“I think his entire affect has been militantly ‘anti-establishment’ in ways that are designed to appeal to 21-year-old Joe Rogan listeners. And I think that is not how you win a broad-scale national election.”

Despite Emerson’s disappointing findings for Vance, he is still ahead in the estimation of the prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket.

On the Democratic side, Emerson placed Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff out in front on 17 percent, 2024 nominee Kamala Harris on 16 percent, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on 15 percent, ex-transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg on 14 percent, California Gov. Gavin Newsom on 11 percent and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear on seven percent.

Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro were all on five percent each.
news.summary: Vice President JD Vance struggling to convince disaffected conservatives he is the right man to lead the GOP into the next presidential election, new survey signals
news.author: Joe Sommerlad

news.title: Young men asked for a future. The GOP offered a lecture.
news.text:
The GOP lost ground across the board in the midterms, but one of the most dramatic swings came from young men. In 2024, Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris among men ages 18 to 29 by 14 points. In 2026, 59% of young male voters backed Democratic House candidates.

Many conservatives adopted the bizarre strategy of mocking young men, especially white young men, before the election, with predictable results. If the Republican Party is to have a future, it must abandon the toxic behavior that so many of its pundits and candidates seem to revel in.

Young white men are the safest demographic to hate, blame, and discriminate against. Society has no taboo about mocking them the way it does for women and minorities. 

After Trump’s stunning 2024 victory, Democrats were devastated. Some conservatives wondered whether Democrats could win nationwide again, while progressive pundits searched for an explanation.

Many leftists concluded that Trump’s surge among young men was critical. Democratic strategists backed a proposed $20 million project to study the language, culture, online habits, and grievances of young men across America.

How Democrats alienated young men is no mystery. The left’s entire ideology is centered on hating and demonizing men. Toxic masculinity and the evils of patriarchy are central tenets of the progressive religion, along with a strong hatred for “whiteness.”

When your entire worldview centers on hating white young men and blaming them for everything bad in your society, it’s naturally going to be difficult to win their support. The party ultimately concluded that while young men were a valuable demographic to win over, they were evil and Democrats really could not change any of their messaging to attract those votes.

The good news for Democrats is that the GOP solved that problem for them. Failing to address affordability and launching a deeply unpopular war managed to damage enthusiasm among young men for Republicans so severely that the voting bloc ended up supporting a party that hates them explicitly. But the problem is far deeper than bad foreign policy or tone-deaf economic messaging.

GOP pundits and candidates adopted a spiteful stance toward young white men while dismissing their concerns. The hatred of young men from Republicans takes a different angle than the hatred from Democrats, but in the end both parties seem to loathe the same demographic for different reasons.

Progressives hate white young men on an ontological level. The very existence of whiteness and masculinity is evil to a Democrat. Young white men may do things that progressives hate, but ultimately, it is the simple fact that they are alive that truly bothers leftists.

This demographic is responsible for every issue America faces, and the only way to resolve those issues is to replace young white men as quickly as possible. The remaining men should be kept weak, servile, and out of power just in case they also manifest these undesirable traits.

For Republicans, the hatred of young white men appears to be built on resentment. Conservatives, especially of the older generations, see themselves as self-made success stories. They tend to ignore that baby boomers grew up in the post-war heyday as America became the dominant global economic force.

They ignore the fact that they bought their homes for pennies on the dollar, attended college when it cost less than a used car, and got hired in major companies before they explicitly discriminated against white men. Republicans see even the most reasonable request for reform to the system as entitled whining from young guys who just cannot be bothered to put in the work.

This attitude manifested itself repeatedly in the messaging before the midterms. After Andrew Kolvet of TPUSA made an off-hand comment about the price of burritos, conservative pundits launched into an absurd campaign to mock young people for caring about affordability. The issue was never simply about the cost of fast food.

The prices of housing, healthcare, education, and energy have exploded and the fact that food — once a cheap staple — suddenly became a luxury item only highlighted the larger problem.

Instead of addressing these valid concerns, conservative pundits mocked young people for using DoorDash or even eating out at all. Surprisingly, the message of “eat rice and beans for the rest of your life while I go on my 20th cruise” did not play well during the election.

The GOP despised young white men so much they even took the time to enshrine it in advertising. Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders ran an ad featuring “Brad,” a doughy white guy who plays video games and eats junk food all day while drawing welfare. Sanders knew young white men were a safe group to mock.

The governor was not in a particularly tight race. Even amidst a blue tsunami, Sanders won Arkansas by 15 points. She ran the ad out of pure spite. Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate in Iowa, said that 29-year-old men living at home were mooching off the federal government. She lost her election.

Young white men are the safest demographic to hate, blame, and discriminate against. Society has no taboo about mocking them the way it does for women and minorities. While the letter of civil rights law technically protects them, the chances of institutions suffering a serious penalty for discrimination against young white men is very low.

Despite spending the last decade documenting the impact of DEI on the education and employment prospects of young white men, conservatives still know that they can only safely blame one group for their ills. Young white men.

Whether it is social taboo, generational scorn, or a combination of both driving this behavior from Republicans, it must stop. Young white men have valid concerns about discrimination, affordability, and employment that deserve to be addressed respectfully.

These men are not just important as a voting bloc, they are important because they are future fathers, entrepreneurs, warriors, and leaders of this country. Young white men are not going anywhere, and neither are their concerns. The GOP can continue to despise them like Democrats do or learn to earn their valuable support by discarding the ridiculous condescension that has been adopted.

news.title: Trump is Putin’s man. This is what Ukraine must do
news.text:
The US is expected to hold further peace talks with Russia and Ukraine in the weeks ahead, but doubts are deepening over whether America will ever be a reliable partner for Kyiv in its war with Moscow.

Donald Trump met Vladimir Putin several times this week at the high-profile summit in China, with the Kremlin saying Putin was in an “excellent mood” after speaking to the US President about issues including the conflict, and Trump confirming that the pair had a “great relationship”. Meanwhile, the US President has been highly critical of Volodymyr Zelensky’s staunch defence of Ukrainian national interests.

Earlier this week, deputy Pentagon chief Elbridge Colby criticised Ukraine for its long-range strikes against Russia. The comments were dismissed by Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, as “stupid” – asking why the US had not made the same criticism of Moscow.

Though Washington transferred primary responsibility for directly aiding Kyiv to Europe in 2025, it has retained an uncomfortable influence over Ukraine – as disruptions with intelligence sharing and the Starshield satellite functioning have made clear. 

And as Trump looks increasingly friendly with Putin on the world stage, the US team has emerged as a proponent of the “might makes right” principle within the peace process, hinting that Ukraine will have to make major concessions over the Donbas region to get an eventual settlement since time is on the Russian side, which is bigger and more powerful.

No wonder that only 7 per cent of Ukrainians approve of US leadership – while 79 per cent of Ukrainians have negative view of it, given the track record of this second Trump administration in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

American domestic politics is actively followed in Ukraine because the country still depends on the US both for aid and for political support, with the White House central to the peace process.

People in Ukraine cheered the Democratic win in the midterm elections, hoping that Congress would from January restore checks and balances in DC. But will it change much for Ukraine?

Democrats will certainly initiate many investigations and hearings, which will consume much of the Trump team’s time and attention. There are solid chances that US negotiators in the trilateral peace process – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – will have to spend more time in Washington after January, answering questions from lawmakers on their dealings instead of mediating Russia-Ukraine negotiations.

The Democratic Party, supported by the internationalist wing of their Republican counterparts, is likely to strictly enforce the Graham act – passed in September to increase diplomatic and economic pressure on Russia. It may even force other sanctions against Moscow. But the federal government can be reticent when legislators force its hand on sanctions – just look at how reluctant the first Trump administration was to implement new harsh measures on Russia.

With the Democrats controlling Congress, Ukrainian authorities might be bolder in defying questionable US initiatives in regard to an eventual peace settlement with Russia. Likewise, with Democratic oversight, there is unlikely to be another situation like one recently in which the Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, spent a month refusing to greenlight a shipment of vital antiaircraft munitions to Ukraine funded by Europe.

Despite Zelensky’s claim this weekend that Starshield restrictions were causing problems in Ukraine, chances are good that, with congressional support, Kyiv will be able to renew the agreement on its usage on favourable terms without major delay under the new Congress in 2027.

But to have consistent support among US lawmakers, Ukraine will need to build its case among newcomers, as many seasoned Republican and Democratic politicians who supported Ukraine will be leaving office. This task will be complicated given the absence of a proper ambassador for Ukraine in DC.

The Democrats would be wise not to appear overly Ukraine-centric in their approach, since that would allow Republicans to easily discredit their opponents as too internationalist and consumed with other nations’ fortunes instead of prioritising US needs. Trump did it in the 2024 campaign against Kamala Harris and it worked with the nationalistic American electorate.

Though there are reports that some political observers expect a $15bn (£11.4bn) package of US aid to Ukraine to be approved by the new Congress, it looks highly unlikely under current conditions in America. Republicans managed to drive the US population to the conclusion that it is primarily Europe’s responsibility to support Ukraine. Returning to the period when the US directly supported Ukraine through Congress as it did under Joe Biden is close to impossible now. Overall, US voters largely supported Democrats during the 2026 midterms, not because they would like to see more interventionist US foreign policy, but because they felt betrayed by those who touted “America First” and then launched a war of choice against Iran, which resulted in higher fuel prices.

Despite pro-Ukrainian sentiments and a desire to balance Trump, a Democrat-controlled Congress won’t solve one of the direst problems facing Ukraine – the acute deficit of US produced Pac-3 MSE interceptors to deal with Russian ballistic missiles because of Iran. The US now has less than 1,000 interceptors, and production rate is approximately around 600 a year. Ukraine’s request for at least 300 fell on deaf ears. A recently signed contract for 500 interceptors for Ukraine will not be implemented until the early 2030s. 

Expectations of a major American tilt towards Ukraine and Europe given the Democratic electoral wave in the US are likely to prove overblown. Congress might restrain the worst instincts of Trump and his team towards Kyiv, and in some cases, legislators might drive a more favourable US agenda for Ukraine – but there are limits to such a proactive approach. Anyone who expects major positive changes in the US approach towards Ukraine in war and diplomacy may be disappointed.

At best, the new US Congress may give Ukraine and Europe a somewhat better environment to more easily adjust to the post-American world, with its demand to take care of ourselves.

news.title: Byron Donalds says 2028 hopefuls must define themselves, rules out own bid
news.text:
Byron Donalds, Republican congressman and incoming Florida governor, said that 2028 hopefuls will need to redefine their own coalitions and not recreate the previous administrations. 

“To be blunt: What I’ve observed in politics, it’s very hard for somebody to try to recreate the previous person’s coalition,” Donalds told Politico at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in part on Thursday. 

Donalds made history as Florida’s first Black governor to be elected to office. President Donald Trump threw his support behind Donalds as did Florida Governor Ron DeSantis after the primary. 

Following devastating midterm election losses for Republicans, which resulted in losing both House and Senate majority, speculation has swirled surrounding who will be the successor to MAGA after Trump is out of office. 

DeSantis’ post-midterm media rounds have sparked intrigue into whether he is considering another bid for the White House. He was asked about a potential 2028 run by CNN’s Jake Tapper after Election Day and said in part that he has not “planned anything.” 

Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Glenn Youngkin, former Republican governor of Virginia, and many more have all been asked about their intentions for running in 2028 on the Republican side.

Similarly, Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and many more have also been asked about their political futures on the Democratic side. 

What To Know

During his conversation with Politico’s Adam Wren, Donalds said that “Whoever the next person is going to be, they’re going to have to — in some respects — redefine and reshape the electorate about what their supportive coalition is.“

“I think trying to go back into trying to recreate what somebody else’s success was, I think is foolhardy,” he added.

Donalds was asked by Politico if his comments were aimed at Vance, and he responded in part that it is “just the reality of politics,” and running on someone else’s coalition “rarely works.”

“I would advise anybody who’s thinking about taking the next step: You got to define yourself,” Donalds also told the outlet on Thursday. “You have to be yourself. You can’t be a facsimile or a carbon copy or shades of gray of somebody else.”

Following the midterm losses, Trump administration officials speculated on why the results unfolded in such a bruising manner. Vance said that after speaking with a pollster, four areas jumped out, including ending the war with Iran, focusing on the cost of living and inflation, putting America first and changing America’s relationship with Israel.

Trump was asked if he had spoken with Vance about 2028 after the midterms and said in part earlier this month, “We’ll see what happens. … You don’t know who’s talking about running. … Maybe he won’t run, I don’t know who’s gonna run.”

Last month, Vance said he thought the president would endorse him should he launch an official 2028 campaign but added they had not discussed it.

Donalds also shot down any potential 2028 run for himself saying to Politico that he is “absolutely” shutting the door on it, adding “it is not happening.”

“I take this job very seriously,” he later added. “I am not looking at another one.”

Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Thursday, “Donalds is saying the obvious out loud. Coalitions are personal. Trump’s is built around him. [Former President Barack] Obama’s was built around him. Trying to photocopy either one usually fails. The next Republican nominee will have to assemble something that fits their own strengths and the electorate of 2028, not 2024. That is basic politics, not a break with Trump.

“His quick no on running himself is also practical. He just won Florida. He has a full term ahead, a legislature to manage, and a record to build. Jumping into a national primary before he has governed would look premature to most voters and donors,” Agranoff added. “It keeps the focus on the job he just got and leaves the 2028 field open for others who are already positioning. It is the kind of clear answer that avoids speculation without creating new problems.”

What Prediction Markets Show

On prediction market Kalshi Thursday night, Vance has a 33 percent chance of winning the GOP presidential nomination. Rubio has 22 percent and DeSantis has 16 percent.

On Polymarket, Vance has 33 percent Thursday night, Rubio has 21 percent, DeSantis has 15 percent and other potential candidates, including Cruz, Youngkin and Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, all have single digits.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins

news.title: 2028 Is Looking Like 2016 but Upside Down
news.text:
The two parties' presidential lineups look a lot like those of the 2015-16 cycle — in reverse.

Republicans emerged from the 2014 midterm elections with large congressional majorities (247 House members and 54 senators). Democrats have emerged from this year's midterm elections with even larger ones (259 House members and 56 senators).

But Democrats then, like Republicans now, had a much smaller field of prospective presidential candidates. Two figures in former President Barack Obama's party towered over the others in visibility and popularity — his vice president, Joe Biden, and his first-term secretary of state, Hillary Clinton.

Recent vice presidents had won the presidency or come close, among them Richard Nixon, Hubert Humphrey, George H.W. Bush and Al Gore. No former secretary of state had won the presidency since James Buchanan in 1856. Yet Obama favored Clinton over Biden.

One reason may have been age. Clinton would have been 69 at the outset of the next presidential term, while Biden would have been 74. That didn't prevent Biden from becoming the consensus choice for the nomination four years later. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who was 75 by the next inauguration, was even older. He entered the primaries from stage left, winning 22 primaries and caucuses and holding Clinton to a 55 percent-43 percent advantage in votes cast for the nomination.

Today's Republican field looks as small as the Democratic field did at the same point in that cycle. It, too, includes a vice president and a secretary of state, with room for a third candidate who is no one's idea of a Washington insider.

Vice President JD Vance is in his first term, while Biden was in his second, and Vance's two years in the Senate pale beside Biden's 36. But Vance has the advantage of youth. He will be just 44 on Inauguration Day in 2029. Like Clinton, Secretary of State Marco Rubio served in the Senate — 14 years in his case, eight in hers. If elected in 2028, he would take the presidential oath at the mature but hardly elderly age of 57.

Rubio's statement that he won't run if Vance does can be read as an attempt to avoid turmoil in the Trump administration — a predictably unattainable goal. In the two weeks since the election, Vance has attributed the Republican rout solely to military action against Iran, which Rubio has supported. President Donald Trump, in turn, has publicly ordered Vance to give his full attention to exposing Democratic corruption in large cities.

Trump's favor may shift, and it may count for less than it once did. The Republican polling firm Echelon Insights reports that 56 percent of Republicans see themselves as party-first and only 36 percent as Trump-first. Another 51 percent say it is time to "move beyond the Trump approach."

The RealClearPolitics average of seven polls on the Republican nomination this fall shows Vance leading Rubio by a less-than-overwhelming margin, 37 percent to 28 percent. Outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL) draws 10 percent.

DeSantis' record of policy success in Florida, the only one of the 10 largest states to remain safely Republican this year, could make him a serious contender. He would be just 50 on Inauguration Day in 2029.

Meanwhile, Democrats, still giddy over their success, could field as many presidential candidates as the 10 Republicans who competed in the 2016 caucuses and primaries. That Republican field included senators from Florida, Kentucky and Texas; current and former governors from Arkansas, Florida, New Jersey and Ohio; a pediatric surgeon from Maryland; a former tech CEO from California; and a real estate developer and reality TV host from New York.

Trump won that crowded contest despite taking positions on trade, war and economic policy far outside those of previous Republican presidents. By the time he won an outright majority in any state, 36 states had already voted.

The Democratic field now taking shape looks something like that Republican field. The RealClearPolitics average of recent polls shows measurable support for 10 candidates. They include governors from California, Illinois, Kentucky and Pennsylvania, senators from Arizona, Georgia and New Jersey, a House member from New York, a former transportation secretary, and former Vice President Kamala Harris, the party's 2024 nominee.

They range widely in age and experience. If Harris took the presidential oath in January 2029, she would be the eighth-oldest person to do so for the first time. Just days would separate her from Zachary Taylor and George H.W. Bush. Only William Henry Harrison, Buchanan, Ronald Reagan, Trump and Biden were older than all three when they first took office. At the other end of the list, either Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), at 41, or Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14), at 39, would be the youngest president ever.

The field could grow or shrink. Someone whose candidacy seems as improbable as Trump's did a dozen years ago could enter the race and win.

America's two political parties have retained their basic characters across centuries. The Republican Party has always centered on people who see themselves, and whom others see, as typical Americans. In a nation that has always been culturally diverse, they have never made up a majority on their own.

The Democrat Party has always been a coalition of outsiders, people who see themselves, and whom others see, as outside the American mainstream. If they hold together, they can form a majority.

When Democrats lack a dominant leader — and Obama, nearly 10 years out of office, no longer seems to play that role — the danger is that the party's disparate constituencies will extract concessions that help candidates win the nomination but cost them votes in the general election.

Transgender advocates' demand for sex-change surgery for prisoners, which Harris docilely endorsed on camera, wounded her candidacy in 2024, perhaps fatally. Other demands from the period Ocasio-Cortez called "Woke 1" included defunding the police, admitting all otherwise illegal aliens who claim asylum, allowing biological men in girls' sports and women's prisons, and requiring masks during the COVID-19 pandemic. Endorsing such demands may help candidates win support in the spring 2028 primaries but prove disastrous in the general election.

Democrats will have a hard time balancing public demands for "affordability" with calls for more public spending from teachers unions and victims' groups. Continued demands for racial quotas and preferences in hiring and political districting may also seem beside the point. The country elected a black president in 2008, and voters just elected a Black Democrat senator in Mississippi and a Black Republican governor in Florida.

In days of yore, local Democratic bosses could grant concessions on some issues and mollify those whose demands they rejected. Today, the very existence of single-issue groups — and their payrolls — depends on wresting concessions from the party on unpopular issues. Popular positions usually don't need paid advocates.

As analysts have noted, most voters in the electorate that gave Democrats large majorities still view the party unfavorably. In the midterm elections, voters could use Democrats as a check on an increasingly disconnected Trump without giving the party full control of the government. In 2028, Democrats will ask for just that, while voters will likely see little risk of Republicans winning the presidency and both chambers of Congress, as they did in 2016 and 2024.

That's why Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston, who have been giving Democrats good advice for more than 30 years, write that "the midterms say little about who will win in 2028" and "do not conclusively show which kind of Democrat would be more electable at the national level in 2028."

Democrats are fortunate that their majorities are large enough to limit the leverage of the Democratic Socialists of America and other leftists in setting policy. But the left has a cheering section in the press and among affluent college graduates, who lately have been the party's largest constituency. Both groups will likely push the party leftward.

None of this is set in stone. Choices yet to be made and events yet to occur will shape the outcome, as they did 10 years ago. Democrats have an opportunity to present an attractive face, but they have flubbed such opportunities before. Republicans, for all their drubbing this year, still have assets that Trump, busy redesigning the White House complex and cleaning the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, has left undeployed.

Michael Barone is a senior political analyst for the Washington Examiner, resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and longtime co-author of The Almanac of American Politics. news.title: Goodbye Electoral College, Hello Totalitarianism, Part One
news.text:
As we all know, the Democratic Party wants to abolish the Electoral College (EC). They might make a big push in the next two years to do so, and it is not impossible that they will succeed. Most Americans are totally clueless about why our Founders established the Electoral College, a matter I will fully discuss in part two of this series. The Democrats are trying to make it all about “democracy” now — which, in one sense, it is, and they might be able to demagogue enough people into abolishing the EC.

Technically, since the Electoral College is part of the election process and ensconced in the Constitution, the Democrats would need a constitutional amendment to abolish it. Technically. In this regard, the problem for them is that they would need 38 states to ratify the amendment, and they almost assuredly don’t have that many at present, and it will probably be several years, at best, before they could muster that number. Most Southern and Western states (minus the Left Coast) would not go for the abolition of the EC by constitutional amendment. So, the Democrats have decided to try an end run around the EC.

They have created this monstrosity called the “National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.” This thing has been around for well over a decade now, and it might be gaining steam. The idea is to find a way to elect the president by popular vote and bypass the EC (if it can’t be eradicated by constitutional amendment). What the NPVIC says is that any state would give all its electoral votes to the candidate who received the most national popular votes, even if that candidate did not win that state’s popular vote. For example, if candidate “A” won the national popular vote, he would get all of a state’s electoral votes even if candidate “B” actually won the state’s popular vote. The state’s “electors” would then be required to vote for candidate “A” when the Electoral College voted on the president. If enough states adopt the NPVIC, the Electoral College, as constitutionally construed, would be negated and bypassed.

So far, 18 states, all (unsurprisingly) very blue, and representing 222 electoral votes, have joined this compact. The newly elected Democrat governor of Nevada, Aaron Ford, hopes to get his state to enact the NPVIC. He has said that the Electoral College must go because it has “racist underpinnings,” and “not only for that reason but because we’ve seen several times now the person who wins the popular vote not win [the presidency] because of the Electoral College.” The Democrats will push this “national popular vote” thing — “the people should decide by popular vote who the president will be.” That’s the approach they are going to hammer — and already are, and it will persuade millions of Americans who, as I said, have absolutely no idea why the Founding Fathers established the Electoral College. news.title: Byron Donalds Says 2028 Hopefuls Must Define Themselves, Rules Out Own Bid
news.text: Byron Donalds, Republican congressman and incoming Florida governor, said that 2028 hopefuls will need to redefine their own coalitions and not recreate the previous administrations. “To be blunt: What I’ve observed in politics, it’s very hard for somebody to try to recreate the previous person’s coalition,” Donalds told Politico at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in part on Thursday. Donalds made history as Florida's first Black governor to be elected to office. President Donald Trump threw his support behind Donalds as did Florida Governor Ron DeSantis after the primary. Following devastating midterm election losses for Republicans, which resulted in losing both House and Senate majority, speculation has swirled surrounding who will be the successor to MAGA after Trump is out of office. DeSantis' post-midterm media rounds have sparked intrigue into whether he is considering another bid for the White House. He was asked about a potential 2028 run by CNN's Jake Tapper after Election Day and said in part that he has not "planned anything." Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Glenn Youngkin, former Republican governor of Virginia, and many more have all been asked about their intentions for running in 2028 on the Republican side. Similarly, Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and many more have also been asked about their political futures on the Democratic side. What To Know During his conversation with Politico's Adam Wren, Donalds said that “Whoever the next person is going to be, they’re going to have to — in some respects — redefine and reshape the electorate about what their supportive coalition is.“ "I think trying to go back into trying to recreate what somebody else’s success was, I think is foolhardy,” he added. Donalds was asked by Politico if his comments were aimed at Vance, and he responded in part that it is "just the reality of politics,” and running on someone else's coalition "rarely works." “I would advise anybody who’s thinking about taking the next step: You got to define yourself,” Donalds also told the outlet on Thursday. “You have to be yourself. You can’t be a facsimile or a carbon copy or shades of gray of somebody else.” Following the midterm losses, Trump administration officials speculated on why the results unfolded in such a bruising manner. Vance said that after speaking with a pollster, four areas jumped out, including ending the war with Iran, focusing on the cost of living and inflation, putting America first and changing America's relationship with Israel. Trump was asked if he had spoken with Vance about 2028 after the midterms and said in part earlier this month, "We'll see what happens. ... You don't know who's talking about running. ... Maybe he won't run, I don't know who's gonna run." Last month, Vance said he thought the president would endorse him should he launch an official 2028 campaign but added they had not discussed it. Donalds also shot down any potential 2028 run for himself saying to Politico that he is "absolutely" shutting the door on it, adding "it is not happening." “I take this job very seriously,” he later added. “I am not looking at another one.” Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Thursday, "Donalds is saying the obvious out loud. Coalitions are personal. Trump’s is built around him. [Former President Barack] Obama’s was built around him. Trying to photocopy either one usually fails. The next Republican nominee will have to assemble something that fits their own strengths and the electorate of 2028, not 2024. That is basic politics, not a break with Trump. "His quick no on running himself is also practical. He just won Florida. He has a full term ahead, a legislature to manage, and a record to build. Jumping into a national primary before he has governed would look premature to most voters and donors," Agranoff added. "It keeps the focus on the job he just got and leaves the 2028 field open for others who are already positioning. It is the kind of clear answer that avoids speculation without creating new problems." What Prediction Markets Show On prediction market Kalshi Thursday night, Vance has a 33 percent chance of winning the GOP presidential nomination. Rubio has 22 percent and DeSantis has 16 percent. On Polymarket, Vance has 33 percent Thursday night, Rubio has 21 percent, DeSantis has 15 percent and other potential candidates, including Cruz, Youngkin and Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, all have single digits.
